Question 1

_______ is the process of selecting appropriate query execution strategy?

  • A. Query graph
  • B. Query optimization
  • C. Query tree
  • D. Query processing

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 5

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.

Study-guide sections

ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

ADB-S01 · Query representations and relational operators

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

ADB-S01 · Query representations and relational operators

Correct answer: B — Query optimization

Selecting an efficient execution strategy is optimization. A tree or graph represents the query; processing is the broader transformation and execution activity.

Evidence in the complete study note

Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.ADB17
Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.ADB17
A query graph represents the predicate relationships of a relational-calculus expression without itself prescribing an operator execution order.ADB-S01

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A graph corresponds to relational calculus, not strategy selection. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

B · correct — The module explicitly defines optimization as choosing an efficient strategy. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

C · incorrect — A query tree represents relational algebra and operations. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

D · incorrect — Processing includes decomposition and execution as well as optimization. (PDF pp. 27, 34.)

Question 2

Which update-timing policy permits a transaction's changes to reach the persistent database before the transaction commits?

  • A. In-Place Update
  • B. Immediate update
  • C. Shadow update
  • D. Deferred update

Adapted from

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 22

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

Study-guide sections

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

Correct answer: B — Immediate update

Immediate update permits a transaction's changes to be written to the persistent database before commit. If that transaction later aborts, recovery may need to undo those changes. Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. In-place update describes overwriting an existing location, while shadow update describes writing a separate version. Those location strategies do not, by their names alone, specify the timing policy requested here. Immediate update need not flush every cache write immediately.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.ADB29
Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.ADB29
In-place update overwrites the original location.ADB29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Describes overwriting the existing location, not the commit-timing policy.

B · correct — Correct: immediate update permits persistent database changes before commit and may require undo.

C · incorrect — Describes writing a separate version while preserving the committed one, not the requested timing policy.

D · incorrect — Deferred update excludes uncommitted changes from the persistent database.

Question 3

Which query-optimization approach applies relational-algebra properties and equivalences to rewrite a query and reduce intermediate work?

  • A. Database storage without query rewriting
  • B. Heuristic approach
  • C. Deterministic execution without query rewriting
  • D. Physical-plan cost estimation

Adapted from

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 26

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Consider which equivalent transformation changes intermediate work and what assumptions preserve meaning.

Study-guide sections

ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

Correct answer: B — Heuristic approach

Heuristic optimization uses algebraic rules to reduce intermediate work, for example applying selective filters earlier, replacing a product plus join predicate with a join and projecting away unneeded columns. Storage and execution without rewriting do not perform those transformations. Cost estimation predicts resources for candidate plans rather than naming the algebraic rewrite approach itself. A practical optimizer can combine rewriting and costing, but the question isolates the rule-based transformation role.

Evidence in the complete study note

Heuristics reduce intermediate work: push selective row filters toward base tables; replace product followed by a join predicate with a join; project unneeded columns away while retaining join/filter columns; reorder inner joins when equivalence permits; reuse common expressions when worthwhile. Split conjunctive selections when each predicate can be applied earlier to its own input.ADB18
A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.ADB19

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: storage without rewriting does not transform the algebraic query representation.

B · correct — Correct: heuristic rewriting uses operator properties and equivalences to reduce intermediate work.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: repeatable execution without rewriting does not apply the requested query transformations.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: cost estimation predicts candidate-plan resource use rather than identifying the algebraic rewrite approach.

Question 4

In which phase of the two phase locking protocol can a transaction obtain locks?

  • A. Release phase
  • B. Roll back phase
  • C. Shrinking phase
  • D. Growing phase

Sources

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 46

  • Computer Science Exit Exam practice questions · Question 38

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.

Study-guide sections

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Correct answer: D — Growing phase

Two-phase locking acquires locks in the growing phase, then releases them in the shrinking phase without acquiring new ones.

Evidence in the complete study note

Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.ADB12
Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.ADB12
Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort.ADB12

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Release is the unlocking portion, not acquisition. (PDF pp. 86.)

B · incorrect — Rollback is not one of the two acquisition/release phases. (PDF pp. 86.)

C · incorrect — Shrinking forbids new locks. (PDF pp. 86.)

D · correct — Growing allows acquisition and forbids release. (PDF pp. 86.)

Question 5

Which one of the following is not problem if concurrency is not controlled properly?

  • A. Lost update problem
  • B. Consistent database
  • C. Incorrect summary
  • D. Dirty read

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 53

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.

Study-guide sections

ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

Correct answer: B — Consistent database

Lost update, temporary update/dirty read, and incorrect summary are concurrency problems. A consistent database is the desired outcome of concurrency control.

Evidence in the complete study note

Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08
Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.ADB06
A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work.ADB06

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Lost update is explicitly a concurrency anomaly. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

B · correct — Consistency is a desired state, so this is the exception. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

C · incorrect — Incorrect summary mixes values from different update stages. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

D · incorrect — Dirty read exposes an update before its transaction has safely committed. (PDF pp. 68, 70, 79.)

Question 6

Which one of the following is not a condition for two operations in a schedule to be said to conflict?

  • A. If they access the same item X
  • B. If they belong to the same transactions
  • C. If Write_item (X) is at least one of the operations
  • D. If they belong to different transactions

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 78

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence.

Study-guide sections

ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

Correct answer: B — If they belong to the same transactions

Conflict requires different transactions, the same item, and at least one write. Membership in the same transaction is therefore the exception.

Evidence in the complete study note

A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict.ADB09

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Accessing the same item is required. (PDF pp. 70, 71.)

B · correct — Same-transaction operations fail the different-transaction requirement. (PDF pp. 70, 71.)

C · incorrect — At least one write is required. (PDF pp. 70, 71.)

D · incorrect — Different transactions is required, so D is not the exception. (PDF pp. 70, 71.)

Question 7

During restart recovery after a crash, which operation removes the database effects of a transaction that had not committed?

  • A. View
  • B. Commit
  • C. Rollback
  • D. Redo

Adapted from

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 79

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required.

Study-guide sections

ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

ADB25 · GRANT, REVOKE and privilege scope

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

ADB25 · GRANT, REVOKE and privilege scope

Correct answer: C — Rollback

Atomicity requires removing the effects of an incomplete transaction after a crash. Rollback performs that undo work, restoring before-images as needed. Commit instead accepts successful transaction effects, and a view is a query representation rather than a recovery action. Redo installs logged after-images to recover missing work; it does not name the removal of uncommitted effects requested here. These actions occur during restart recovery after the system is operating again.

Evidence in the complete study note

Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects. Rollback handles failed/uncommitted work; redo preserves committed work missing from pages; checkpoints reduce log-search work; backups provide another stored copy.ADB26
Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.ADB27
A view is a stored query definition, not encryption.ADB25

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: a view is not an operation that reverses transaction effects.

B · incorrect — Incorrect: commit accepts transaction effects rather than undoing the incomplete work.

C · correct — Correct: rollback undoes the effects of the uncommitted transaction.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: redo installs logged after-images; the requested removal requires undo/rollback.

Question 8

A system is in a ______ state if there exists a set of transactions such that every transaction in the set is waiting for another transaction in the set.

  • A. Idle
  • B. Waiting
  • C. Deadlock
  • D. Ready

Source

  • MOE Computer Science Exit Exam · 2016 · Question 81

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

Study-guide sections

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

Correct answer: C — Deadlock

Mutual waiting among transactions for locks held by one another is a deadlock condition.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13
Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.ADB13
A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.ADB13

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Idle does not express mutual lock waiting. (PDF pp. 87.)

B · incorrect — Waiting alone need not involve a cycle. (PDF pp. 87.)

C · correct — Deadlock is mutual waiting that prevents progress. (PDF pp. 87.)

D · incorrect — Ready does not describe transactions blocked on one another. (PDF pp. 87.)

Question 9

Users may request permitted aggregates but must not infer protected individual values by subtracting overlapping aggregate answers. Which security measure specifically addresses this indirect-disclosure threat?

  • A. Inference control
  • B. Access control
  • C. Integrity control
  • D. Encryption
  • E. None of the above

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 15

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Identify whether the scenario concerns identity, permission, disclosure or valid values.

Study-guide sections

ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

Correct answer: A — A. Inference control

Inference control targets learning protected individual facts from aggregate answers. For example, subtracting a sum excluding one person from a sum including that person can reveal their value even when their row is hidden. Ordinary access control grants or denies actions, integrity validates data and encryption protects encoded content. The specified indirect-disclosure threat identifies inference control specifically.

Evidence in the complete study note

Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions. Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions. A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges. A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction.ADB24
Inference control concerns learning protected individual facts indirectly from allowed aggregate answers.ADB24
Releasing SUM for a group and SUM for the same group excluding one known person may disclose that person's value by subtraction.ADB24

Choice by choice

A · correct — This directly prevents disclosure of individual facts inferred from allowed aggregates.

B · incorrect — Authorization alone does not prevent inference from otherwise allowed answers.

C · incorrect — Integrity constrains valid data rather than indirect disclosure.

D · incorrect — Encryption does not stop an authorized user combining decrypted aggregate answers.

E · incorrect — Inference control directly matches the threat.

Question 10

Which approach rewrites a query's internal representation using relational-algebra equivalences, without relying on integrity-constraint deductions or comparison of estimated plan costs?

  • A. Systematic plan-cost estimation
  • B. Semantic query optimization
  • C. Cost Estimation
  • D. Heuristic rules
  • E. Both A and C

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 16

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Consider which equivalent transformation changes intermediate work and what assumptions preserve meaning.

Study-guide sections

ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

Correct answer: D — Heuristic rules

Heuristic rules rewrite algebraic representations using equivalences, such as applying suitable selections early or replacing a product followed by a join condition with a join. Semantic optimization additionally reasons from trusted constraints. Cost estimation predicts resources for candidate plans, and doing that systematically remains a costing activity. The stem isolates equivalence-based rewriting without those other bases, so D is correct and combining the two cost-estimation descriptions does not change the answer.

Evidence in the complete study note

Heuristics reduce intermediate work: push selective row filters toward base tables; replace product followed by a join predicate with a join; project unneeded columns away while retaining join/filter columns; reorder inner joins when equivalence permits; reuse common expressions when worthwhile. Split conjunctive selections when each predicate can be applied earlier to its own input.ADB18
Semantic optimization additionally uses trusted constraints, such as a key proving a join cannot multiply matching rows. Cost-based optimization estimates candidate plans instead of relying on rules alone.ADB18
A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic.ADB19

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: systematic cost estimation predicts plan costs rather than performing the specified equivalence-based rewriting.

B · incorrect — Incorrect: semantic optimization additionally uses trusted constraints, which the stem excludes.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: cost estimation compares resource predictions for candidate plans.

D · correct — Correct: heuristic rules apply the stated relational-algebra equivalences.

E · incorrect — Incorrect: A and C both describe costing, not the isolated algebraic-rewrite approach.

Question 11

Which of the following is not true about locks?

  • A. Locks with large granularity are easier for the DBMS to administer.
  • B. Locks with small granularity cause more conflicts.
  • C. Locks with large granularity produce fewer details for the DBMS to track.
  • D. Locks may have a table-level granularity.
  • E. Locks may have a database-level granularity.

Source

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 17

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.

Study-guide sections

ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

Correct answer: B — Locks with small granularity cause more conflicts.

Fine granularity raises concurrency, whereas coarse granularity locks more data with fewer lock entries. Thus the claim that smaller units cause more conflicts reverses the tradeoff.

Evidence in the complete study note

Fine-grained row locks permit more independent operations but require tracking many locks. Coarse table/database locks simplify management but block unrelated rows and reduce concurrency. Intention locks advertise planned descendant locks in a hierarchy; escalation replaces many small locks with a coarser one. Small granularity does not inherently cause more logical conflicts. Choose granularity from contention and management overhead, not a universal rule.ADB16

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — A single coarse lock can replace many fine locks and reduce management work. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

B · correct — Fine units allow more independent access, so this is the false claim. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

C · incorrect — Coarse locks reduce the number of entries tracked. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

D · incorrect — The file/relation granularity in the hierarchy permits table-level locking. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

E · incorrect — Entire-database locking is expressly listed. (PDF pp. 83, 95.)

Question 12

For every transaction T participating in the schedule, if all the operations of T are executed consecutively in the schedule. The schedule is

  • A. Cascaded schedule
  • B. Serial schedule
  • C. Cascadeless schedule
  • D. Recoverable schedule
  • E. None

Source

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 18

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence.

Study-guide sections

ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

ADB10 · Recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

ADB10 · Recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules

Correct answer: B — Serial schedule

Consecutive execution of every transaction's operations is the definition of a serial schedule. Recoverability and cascadelessness instead constrain dependencies on commits.

Evidence in the complete study note

A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict.ADB09
Recoverable means if Tj reads Ti's value, Tj cannot commit before Ti commits.ADB10
Cascadeless means a transaction reads only values written by committed transactions, avoiding cascading aborts.ADB10

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Cascading concerns dependent rollbacks, not contiguous execution. (PDF pp. 72, 71.)

C · incorrect — Cascadeless means reading only committed writes. (PDF pp. 72, 71.)

D · incorrect — Recoverable constrains commit order after a read dependency. (PDF pp. 72, 71.)

Question 14

Which update-timing policy keeps a transaction's uncommitted changes outside the persistent database until commit?

  • A. Undo
  • B. In-place modification
  • C. Immediate-modification
  • D. Deferred-modification

Adapted from

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 20

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

Study-guide sections

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

Correct answer: D — Deferred-modification

Deferred modification keeps uncommitted updates outside the persistent database. If the transaction fails before commit, those database pages do not require undo for its changes; redo can still be needed after commit in a no-force system. Immediate modification permits precommit persistent changes. In-place modification describes overwriting the original location without specifying the commit timing, while undo is an action that reverses applied effects. D therefore names the requested timing policy.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.ADB29
In-place update overwrites the original location.ADB29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: undo reverses effects already applied rather than naming a policy postponing them.

B · incorrect — Incorrect: in-place modification specifies overwriting location, not postponement until commit.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: immediate modification permits persistent changes before commit.

D · correct — Correct: deferred modification keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database.

Question 15

Which one of the following is false?

  • A. In object-oriented database, data are stored as collections of rows and tables
  • B. In relational database, data are perceived by users as tables
  • C. Object oriented database allows object identification and communication
  • D. Object oriented database allows reusability of objects
  • E. None of the above

Source

  • Addis Ababa University mock exam · Question 21

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Distinguish an object instance from its class, attribute values and persistent identity.

Study-guide sections

ADB01 · Objects, identity, classes and persistence

ADB02 · Encapsulation, abstraction and object associations

ADB03 · Inheritance, polymorphism and safe substitutability

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB01 · Objects, identity, classes and persistence

ADB02 · Encapsulation, abstraction and object associations

ADB03 · Inheritance, polymorphism and safe substitutability

Correct answer: A — The rows-and-tables claim is false for the object-oriented model.

An OODBMS primarily models persistent objects with identity, state and behavior, rather than relational rows and tables. Objects communicate through methods and object references, and inheritance supports reuse. Relational presentation as tables is the contrasting model. Therefore A is the false statement.

Evidence in the complete study note

An object combines identity, state and behavior. A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance. The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime. Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.ADB01
It does not primarily present objects as rows and tables.ADB01
An object-relational DBMS extends a relational system with richer types; ORM maps programming objects into relational tables.ADB01

Choice by choice

A · correct — This is false: an OODBMS primarily models persistent objects rather than relational rows and tables.

B · incorrect — Presenting relations as tables describes the relational contrast correctly.

C · incorrect — Object identity and method-based collaboration are supported object-model concepts.

D · incorrect — Inheritance and reusable object behavior support reuse, so this is not the false statement.

E · incorrect — A is false, so none of the above cannot answer this negative question.

Question 16

27.----------is a collection of multiple logically related database distributed over a computer network.

  • A. Data Fragmentation
  • B. Distributed Database
  • C. Data Allocation
  • D. Data Replication

Sources

  • Computer Science model exam · Question 27

  • University of Gondar model exam · Question 27

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration.

Study-guide sections

ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

Correct answer: B — Distributed Database

A distributed database is a coordinated collection of logically related data across networked sites. Fragmentation divides a relation into row or column subsets; replication creates copies; allocation chooses the sites storing fragments or copies. These are design decisions within a distributed database rather than alternative names for the whole collection. Distribution does not require every fragment to be replicated, and the question's definition identifies the database as a whole.

Evidence in the complete study note

A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system.ADB33
Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation.ADB36
Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.ADB37

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: fragmentation splits relations into subsets rather than naming the entire networked collection.

B · correct — Correct: a distributed database is the coordinated logically related data collection across networked sites.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: allocation assigns fragments or copies to sites; it is a placement decision.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: replication creates copies and is a design choice rather than the definition of the collection.

Question 17

ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.ADB06

ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

Correct answer: A — Recovery measures

A checkpoint synchronizes database and log so recovery need not search the entire history. Its purpose is recovery work reduction.

A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.ADB30
Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.ADB30
Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem.ADB30

Question 19

Which of the following is not a recovery technique?

  • A. ARIES Algorithm
  • B. Two-phase commit
  • C. Immediate update
  • D. Deferred update

ADB39 · Distributed atomic commit and Oracle commit points

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB39 · Distributed atomic commit and Oracle commit points

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB31 · ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

Correct answer: B — Two-phase commit

Deferred update, immediate update, and ARIES are recovery approaches. Two-phase commit coordinates the distributed commit decision; it is the intended exception among the named recovery algorithms, though commit protocols also support distributed recovery.

Evidence in the complete study note

Two-phase commit (2PC) first asks participants to prepare and durably promise they can commit. If all vote yes, the coordinator records commit durably and tells participants; otherwise it decides abort. A prepared participant must retain enough state to obey the final decision. Coordinator/communication failure can leave it in doubt and block progress until the decision is learned. Timeout after preparation is not permission to invent a commit or abort.ADB39
2PC coordinates atomic outcome; locking/other concurrency protocols provide isolation.ADB39
Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.ADB29

D · incorrect — Deferred update is a recovery scheme. (PDF pp. 107, 109, 123.)

Question 20

Which of the following is not true about OODBMS (object-oriented database management system).

Study-guide sections

ADB01 · Objects, identity, classes and persistence

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB01 · Objects, identity, classes and persistence

Correct answer: C — Relation is not the defining concept of an OODBMS.

The defining unit of an object database is an object with identity, state and behavior. ADB01 explains both persistence beyond program execution and identifier stability throughout an object lifetime. Relation is instead the characteristic abstraction of the relational model. Thus C is the one statement that fails to describe an OODBMS.

Evidence in the complete study note

An object combines identity, state and behavior. A class specifies the attributes and operations of its instances; an object is one instance. The object identifier (OID) distinguishes objects independently of their attribute values and remains stable over that object's lifetime. Two objects can have equal values and different identities; changing a name does not create a new identity.ADB01
Persistence lets an object survive beyond the program execution that created it.ADB01
Complex CAD or multimedia structures can suit an object model, but many-to-many relationships alone do not require abandoning relational design.ADB01

Choice by choice

B · incorrect — An OODBMS provides persistence so objects survive the program execution that created them.

D · incorrect — The object identifier remains stable throughout the lifetime of its object.

Question 21

Which optimization approach uses algebraic rules, such as pushing suitable selections before joins, to choose an operation order without exhaustively enumerating plans or comparing estimated costs?

  • A. Semantic query optimization based on trusted constraints
  • B. Heuristic- based
  • C. Cost estimation
  • D. Exhaustive search

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · Question 37

  • University of Gondar model exam · Question 37

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Consider which equivalent transformation changes intermediate work and what assumptions preserve meaning.

Study-guide sections

ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

Correct answer: B — Heuristic- based

Heuristic optimization orders or rewrites operations using algebraic rules intended to reduce intermediate work. Applying suitable selections early is a typical example. Semantic optimization additionally uses trusted constraints, cost estimation predicts resource usage for candidate strategies, and exhaustive search enumerates alternatives rather than selecting a small set through rules alone. Although practical optimizers can combine these methods, the stated stem asks specifically for rule-based algebraic ordering, making B unique.

Evidence in the complete study note

Heuristics reduce intermediate work: push selective row filters toward base tables; replace product followed by a join predicate with a join; project unneeded columns away while retaining join/filter columns; reorder inner joins when equivalence permits; reuse common expressions when worthwhile. Split conjunctive selections when each predicate can be applied earlier to its own input.ADB18
Semantic optimization additionally uses trusted constraints, such as a key proving a join cannot multiply matching rows. Cost-based optimization estimates candidate plans instead of relying on rules alone.ADB18

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: this alternative bases deductions on trusted constraints rather than the isolated algebraic ordering rules.

B · correct — Correct: heuristic optimization orders operations through algebraic rules such as early selection.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: cost estimation predicts candidate-plan resources instead of the specified rule-only choice.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: exhaustive search enumerates alternatives, which the stem explicitly excludes.

All database actions occurring or none occurring is atomicity, the first ACID property.

Evidence in the complete study note

A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Question 23

A transaction is still active when one of its changes is written into the persistent database. Which update-timing policy permits this?

  • A. Deferred-Update
  • B. In-place update
  • C. Immediate-Update
  • D. Undo

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 9

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

Study-guide sections

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

Correct answer: C — Immediate-Update

Immediate update permits persistent database changes while the transaction is still active, before commit. An abort may therefore require undo. Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. In-place update describes overwriting a location rather than the commit-timing policy, and undo is the reversal of applied effects. The question concerns which timing policy permits the observed precommit write, not whether all immediate-update systems must flush every cache change immediately.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.ADB29
In-place update overwrites the original location.ADB29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: deferred update excludes uncommitted changes from the persistent database.

B · incorrect — Incorrect: in-place update describes overwriting the existing location rather than the commit-timing policy.

C · correct — Correct: immediate update permits persistent changes before commit.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: undo reverses effects; it is not the update-timing policy.

Question 24

Which of the following occurs when a transaction cannot proceed for an indefinite period while other transactions in the system continue normally?

  • A. Starvation
  • B. Deadlock
  • C. checkpoint
  • D. lock point

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 25

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

Study-guide sections

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

Correct answer: A — Starvation

Starvation means indefinite postponement of a transaction while other transactions continue. It can result from repeated waiting or repeated victim selection without any waiting cycle. Deadlock instead involves a cycle of mutually blocked transactions. A checkpoint records recovery state, and the lock point in two-phase locking is the instant a transaction acquires its final lock. Neither is the name of indefinite unfair postponement, so A remains the unique answer.

Evidence in the complete study note

Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.ADB13
The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained.ADB12
A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.ADB30

Choice by choice

A · correct — Correct: indefinite postponement while others proceed is starvation.

B · incorrect — Incorrect: deadlock requires a waiting cycle, which is not required for starvation.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: a checkpoint records durable recovery state; it is not an indefinite waiting condition.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: the lock point is the instant the transaction acquires its final lock in 2PL.

Study-guide references

ADB04 · Object type constructors

Correct answer: D — Array is not an atom constructor.

ADB04 lists integer, real, Boolean and string as examples of basic atomic values. An array instead supplies indexed positions and is a collection constructor, even when a programming variable holds it as one value. Consequently integers, reals and strings fit the atom category while an array is the requested exception.

In a common object model, an object is described by (OID,type constructor,state). An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string. A tuple constructor groups named component values into one structured record, such as (Street:'A',City:'B'). It is not a collection of records.ADB04
An array is not an atomic constructor merely because stored as one programming variable.ADB04
A set is an unordered collection without duplicates; a bag allows duplicates; a list has order; an array provides indexed positions.ADB04

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — An integer is explicitly listed as a basic atomic value.

C · incorrect — A string is a basic atomic value under the object-model convention used here.

Question 26

A system crashes again during ARIES recovery. Durable WAL, pageLSNs and compensation log records survive; storage is intact. No checkpoints were taken. Which statement correctly describes the second restart?

  • A. The same undo and redo list will be used while recovering again
  • B. The database will become inconsistent
  • C. Durable compensation records and pageLSNs preserve recovery progress, so already-installed actions can be skipped or safely redone as required.
  • D. The system cannot any further

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 53

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Trace durable recovery metadata and what progress survives a second crash.

Study-guide sections

ADB31 · ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB31 · ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

Correct answer: C — C. Durable compensation records and pageLSNs preserve recovery progress, so already-installed actions can be skipped or safely redone as required.

ARIES records recovery progress in durable metadata. PageLSNs help determine whether a redo action is already installed, and compensation records preserve undo progress and its continuation. A second restart can therefore recover safely without assuming that the same undo and redo work lists recur. Lack of checkpoints may increase scanning work, but it does not erase this progress or make further recovery impossible.

Evidence in the complete study note

ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table. Analysis reconstructs active/loser transactions and dirty-page information. Redo repeats history, starting from the relevant earliest dirty-page update; pageLSNs help skip already-installed actions. Undo reverses loser transactions.ADB31
This makes recovery restartable: after a second crash, durable undo progress need not be undone again as if no progress occurred.ADB31
Compensation log records (CLRs) describe undo actions and their continuation information.ADB31

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Durable progress can change the required work, so identical lists are not guaranteed.

B · incorrect — Restartable recovery does not make inconsistency inevitable.

C · correct — PageLSNs and durable CLRs support safe continuation after repeated crashes.

D · incorrect — ARIES can restart using surviving durable recovery metadata.

Question 27

The rigorous two-phase locking protocol permits releasing all locks at the__________

  • A. Beginning of the transaction
  • B. During the execution of transaction
  • C. End of transaction
  • D. Never in the life-time of transaction

Source

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 59

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.

Study-guide sections

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Correct answer: C — At transaction end, on commit or abort.

Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until commit or abort, unlike basic 2PL, which permits release in its shrinking phase. FDB-style early release would allow interference before completion and would not meet rigorous locking. The locks are eventually released at the transaction boundary, so never is also false.

Evidence in the complete study note

Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort. Rigorous 2PL retains both shared and exclusive locks until that point. Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock. It requires knowing the lock set and can reduce concurrency. Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.ADB12

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Releasing locks at the beginning would not protect the transaction's later accesses.

B · incorrect — Rigorous 2PL does not permit early release during ongoing transaction execution.

C · correct — Both shared and exclusive locks remain held until commit or abort ends the transaction.

D · incorrect — Locks are released at completion; the protocol does not hold them forever.

The committed state guarantees persistent changes. Partially committed only signals the end of read/write operations and does not yet ensure permanence.

Evidence in the complete study note

Active means operations are executing. Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. Committed means commitment succeeded. A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt. Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions.ADB06

Question 29

Let transaction T1 has obtained a shared mode lock S on data item Y and transaction T2 has obtained an exclusive lock X on data item Z , according to the above statement which one is correct?

  • A. T1 can read Y but cannot write Y
  • B. T2 can read Z but cannot write Z
  • C. T1 can read Z but cannot write Z
  • D. T2 can read and write item Y

Source

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 67

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

Study-guide sections

ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

Correct answer: A — T1 can read Y but cannot write Y

Shared locks permit reads but not updates. Exclusive locks permit both reading and updating while excluding other transactions' locks on that item.

Evidence in the complete study note

A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.ADB11
A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks.ADB11
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.ADB11

A · correct — T1's shared lock authorizes reading Y, not writing it. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

B · incorrect — T2's exclusive lock permits both read and update of Z. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

C · incorrect — T1 cannot read Z while another transaction holds its exclusive lock. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

D · incorrect — T2 cannot obtain an exclusive write lock on Y while T1 holds its shared lock. (PDF pp. 82, 83.)

Question 30

Which claim about deadlock prevention and starvation is false?

  • A. In conservative 2PL, starvation may occur
  • B. Wound–wait guarantees starvation freedom regardless of restart priorities or scheduling fairness
  • C. Deadlock can be prevented by wait-die
  • D. Some deadlock-prevention methods may cause starvation

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 84

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.

Study-guide sections

ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

Correct answer: B — Wound–wait guarantees starvation freedom regardless of restart priorities or scheduling fairness

Deadlock freedom does not itself guarantee that each transaction eventually completes. Wound–wait uses transaction age to decide whether a requester waits or aborts a younger holder, but a starvation-freedom argument also needs appropriate restart priorities, fair scheduling and holders that eventually finish. Its unconditional guarantee in B is therefore false. Conservative 2PL can postpone a transaction indefinitely under unfair admission, and wait–die prevents waiting cycles. Some prevention policies can cause repeated waiting or victimization.

Evidence in the complete study note

Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive. Starvation avoidance additionally assumes holders eventually finish and scheduling is fair.ADB14
Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.ADB13

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — True: conservative 2PL prevents cycles but does not by itself guarantee fair admission.

B · correct — Correct selection: the unconditional starvation-freedom claim omits necessary progress and priority assumptions.

C · incorrect — True: wait–die is a timestamp-based deadlock-prevention policy.

D · incorrect — True: preventing deadlock can still leave a transaction repeatedly postponed or aborted.

Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Question 32

A lock wait-for graph may contain several independent deadlock cycles. Which termination methods guarantee eliminating all deadlock cycles? Assume each aborted transaction is undone and releases its locks. Select all that apply. 'Half' and 'single' mean arbitrary selections without a repeated cycle check.

  • A. Abort all deadlocked transaction
  • B. Abort half of the deadlocked transaction
  • C. Aborting single deadlocked transactio
  • D. Aborting one transaction at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam · 2015 · Question 93

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

Study-guide sections

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

Correct answers (select all): A, D — A. Abort all deadlocked transaction; D. Aborting one transaction at a time until the deadlock cycle is eliminated

Aborting all deadlocked transactions removes every participating wait, although it wastes work. A more selective complete method aborts a suitable victim, releases its locks and repeats until no cycles remain. An arbitrary half of the participants can leave a cycle intact, and one arbitrary victim may resolve only one of several independent cycles. The guarantee therefore applies to A and D.

Evidence in the complete study note

Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13
A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp.ADB13
Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.ADB13

Choice by choice

A · correct — Removing all deadlocked participants eliminates all their cycles.

B · incorrect — An arbitrary half may miss an entire remaining cycle.

C · incorrect — One victim need not break other independent cycles.

D · correct — Repeated victim selection and graph checking continues until every cycle is gone.

ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

Correct answer: B — Lost update

Both transactions reading the original value lets a later write overwrite the earlier transaction's update; that update is lost.

Evidence in the complete study note

Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Dirty read concerns uncommitted values from another transaction. (PDF pp. 68, 70.)

B · correct — Lost update matches the stale-original-value overwrite. (PDF pp. 68, 70.)

C · incorrect — Incorrect summary combines differently timed values in an aggregate. (PDF pp. 68, 70.)

D · incorrect — Unrepeatable read concerns a later reread seeing a changed value. (PDF pp. 68, 70.)

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

ADB07 · Read/write operations, buffers and log records

Correct answer: D — Transaction processing system

The transaction processing system contains the scheduler and recovery managers. Its scheduling ensures concurrent individual actions have a net effect equivalent to one-at-a-time execution.

Evidence in the complete study note

A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively.ADB09

Question 38

In two-phase locking (2PL), during which phase may a transaction acquire locks but not release any?

  • B. Commit phase
  • C. . Validation phase
  • D. Shrinking phase

Source

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 5

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

Correct answer: A — Growing phase

The growing phase acquires locks without releasing any. Shrinking starts with release and prohibits new acquisitions.

Evidence in the complete study note

Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. Question 39

Assume durable logs and serializable concurrency control, but no checkpoints or other valid log-truncation boundary. In a high-transaction system using deferred update, which recovery cost can grow after long uptime?

  • A. Recovery may require scanning a very long accumulated log
  • B. Increased disk I/O due to frequent page copying
  • C. Shared locks cannot be used
  • D. View serializability cannot be ensured

Adapted from

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 28

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.

Study-guide sections

ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Correct answer: A — Recovery may require scanning a very long accumulated log

Checkpoints record recovery state so recovery need not inspect the entire accumulated history. Without a checkpoint or another valid truncation boundary, the log that must be searched can grow throughout a long-running workload. Deferred update does not remove that problem. It specifies when persistent changes occur, not a requirement to copy shadow pages or a prohibition on shared locks. Serializability is enforced by the assumed concurrency-control mechanism, rather than by the existence of checkpoints.

Evidence in the complete study note

A fuzzy checkpoint permits ongoing transactions and records active-transaction and dirty-page information without forcing all pages simultaneously. Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position. A checkpoint is neither a full backup nor an automatic commit of active transactions. Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem.ADB30
Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO.ADB29
Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.ADB12

Choice by choice

A · correct — Correct: without a recovery boundary, a long-running system may need to inspect a very large accumulated log.

B · incorrect — Incorrect: deferred update describes timing and does not require frequent shadow-page copying.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: deferring persistent writes does not prohibit shared-lock concurrency control.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: serializability is enforced by the assumed concurrency control; a checkpoint limits recovery work rather than determining schedule equivalence.

Which type of fragmentation in a distributed database divides a relation into subrelations defined by subsets of its columns, normally repeating a key to support reconstruction?

  • A. Replication
  • B. Location
  • C. Horizontal
  • D. Vertical

Adapted from

  • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 82

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.

Study-guide sections

ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

Correct answer: D — Vertical

Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets into separate fragments. Repeating an appropriate key or row identifier allows a join to reconstruct the original rows without spurious combinations. Horizontal fragmentation instead selects subsets of rows, reconstructed by union. Replication creates copies rather than dividing the relation by attributes. Location transparency hides where data resides; it does not name the column-splitting design operation. The corrected category therefore supports the existing vertical-fragmentation answer.

Evidence in the complete study note

Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
Location transparency hides which site holds a named object.ADB35
Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.ADB37

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Replication creates copies of data rather than splitting a relation into column subsets.

B · incorrect — Location transparency hides placement details; it is not a fragmentation method.

C · incorrect — Horizontal fragmentation partitions rows, not columns.

D · correct — Correct: vertical fragmentation splits columns and normally repeats a reconstruction key.

Question 42

In two-phase locking, which phase permits releasing existing locks but forbids acquiring new locks?

  • A. Expanding phase
  • B. Waiting phase
  • C. Shrinking phase
  • D. All of the above

Adapted from

  • National Exit Exam practice questions · Question 7

  • Computer Science Exit Exam practice collection · Question 65

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.

Study-guide sections

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

Correct answer: C — Shrinking phase

Two-phase locking divides lock use into a growing phase and a shrinking phase. During growing, a transaction may acquire or upgrade locks; once it releases a lock, it enters shrinking and cannot acquire any new lock. Waiting describes delay on a conflicting request, not a separate 2PL phase defined by releasing locks. Because the growing phase allows acquisition instead of release, the all-of-the-above alternative also fails.

Evidence in the complete study note

Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.ADB12

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: the growing/expanding phase acquires locks and does not release them.

B · incorrect — Incorrect: waiting on a conflicting request is a delay condition, not the formal 2PL release phase.

C · correct — Correct: shrinking permits release while forbidding new acquisitions.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: the growing phase does not meet the release/no-new-lock rule.

Question 45

Which listed approaches use both undo and redo? Interpret Immediate Update as the conventional steal/no-force logged model and Deferred Update as no-steal/no-force; use the course's ARIES definition. Select all that apply.

  • A. Immediate Update
  • B. Deferred Update
  • C. ARIES Algorithm
  • D. None

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 5

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Determine whether uncommitted changes or unflushed committed changes may exist on persistent pages.

Study-guide sections

ADB28 · Steal and force determine recovery work

ADB31 · ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB28 · Steal and force determine recovery work

ADB31 · ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

Correct answers (select all): A, C — A. Immediate Update; C. ARIES Algorithm

Steal allows uncommitted changes to reach persistent pages, creating a possible need for undo. No-force allows committed changes to remain buffered, creating a possible need for redo. Immediate update under the specified combined policy therefore needs both. ARIES also performs redo and then undoes losers. The specified deferred no-steal/no-force model needs redo but no undo, so it does not qualify.

Evidence in the complete study note

Steal permits a page with uncommitted changes to be written to disk; hence recovery may need undo. No-steal prevents those uncommitted effects reaching the persistent database. Force writes a transaction's updated data pages at commit; no-force permits committed dirty pages to remain buffered, hence recovery may need redo.ADB28
For the conventional page/log model: steal/no-force needs undo and redo; steal/force needs undo but no redo; no-steal/no-force needs redo but no undo; no-steal/force needs neither data-page undo nor redo after a system crash.ADB28
Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO.ADB29

Choice by choice

B · incorrect — The specified deferred policy prevents persistent uncommitted effects and needs redo only.

C · correct — ARIES repeats history with redo and reverses losers with undo.

D · incorrect — Two listed approaches use both actions.

Question 46

Which recovery mechanism preserves the committed page map while writing modified pages elsewhere, then atomically installs a new map at commit as an alternative to conventional log-based recovery?

  • A. Disk recovery
  • B. Shadow paging
  • C. Deferred update
  • D. Crash recovery

Adapted from

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 30

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

Study-guide sections

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

Correct answer: B — Shadow paging

Shadow paging preserves the committed page map and writes modified pages to separate locations. Once the required pages are durable, commit atomically installs the new map; before that point, recovery can use the old committed map. Deferred update instead describes postponing persistent database changes until commit and does not itself specify this page-map mechanism. Disk recovery and crash recovery name recovery domains or events, not the particular algorithm requested.

Evidence in the complete study note

In-place update overwrites the original location. Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version. Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable. Before commit, a crash uses the old map. It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.ADB29
Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO.ADB29

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Incorrect: disk recovery describes a recovery domain, not the specified preserved-page-map mechanism.

B · correct — Correct: shadow paging preserves the committed map and installs the new map atomically at commit.

C · incorrect — Incorrect: deferred update specifies commit timing, not this copy-on-write page-map algorithm.

D · incorrect — Incorrect: crash recovery describes recovery after an event rather than the particular page-map mechanism.

What is the objective of a Serializable schedule?

  • A. Find a Non-serial schedule that allows the interleaving of a transaction and produces the same result as a serial schedule.
  • B. Find a Serial schedule that allows the interleaving of a transaction and produces the same result as a serial schedule.
  • C. Find a Serial schedule that doesn't allow the interleaving of a transaction and produces the same result as a serial schedule.
  • D. Find a Non-serial schedule that doesn't allow the interleaving of a transaction and produces the same result as a serial schedule.

Source

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 66

Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence.

Study-guide sections

ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

Correct answer: A — Find a Non-serial schedule that allows the interleaving of a transaction and produces the same result as a serial schedule.

Serial schedules run each transaction consecutively. Serializability permits nonserial interleaving while preserving the effect of a complete serial schedule (p.72). A expresses this concurrency objective.

Evidence in the complete study note

A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict.ADB09

Choice by choice

A · correct — Interleaving plus serial-equivalent effect meets the objective.

B · incorrect — A serial schedule cannot interleave transactions as claimed.

C · incorrect — This describes serial execution, not the benefit of serializable interleaving.

D · incorrect — Nonserial execution is distinguished by departure from consecutive transaction execution; this denies the intended interleaving.

ADB01 · Objects, identity, classes and persistence

Correct answers (select all): B, C, D — B. Type constructor is used to create a new object.; C. Tuple is a collection of records.; D. The atom constructor is a multi-value constructor.

An OID remains stable over the object's lifetime, so A is true. A data-model type constructor specifies the shape of a value rather than executing creation of a new object. A tuple groups named components into one structured record, while an atom is one basic value. B, C and D therefore state incorrect properties under the specified convention.

In a common object model, an object is described by (OID,type constructor,state). An atom is one basic value, such as an integer, real, Boolean or string. Question 52

Assume transaction A holds a shared lock R. If transaction B also requests for a shared lock on R

  • A. It will result in a deadlock situation
  • B. It will be granted as soon as it is released by A
  • C. It will immediately be granted
  • D. It will immediately be rejected

Source

  • Computer Science model exam 2 · Question 85

Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

Study-guide sections

ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

Correct answer: C — It will immediately be granted

The shared-mode rule permits more than one transaction to hold a read lock on X, while excluding write locks (p.82). With only A’s shared lock specified, B’s shared request is compatible.

Evidence in the complete study note

A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.ADB11
One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.ADB11
The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests.ADB11

Choice by choice

A · incorrect — Two compatible shared requests do not produce the stated deadlock.

B · incorrect — Waiting for A is unnecessary for compatible reads.

C · correct — The shared request is compatible and may be granted immediately under the stated conditions.

D · incorrect — The shared rule supplies no rejection condition here.

Study-guide references

Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08

Question 54

Which sequence matches the course's logical query-processing pipeline for a SELECT, from checking the request to returning its result?

  • A. Parsing and semantic analysis → logical translation → query optimization → evaluation → output

ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

Answer & Detailed Explanation

Study-guide references

ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

Correct answer: A — A. Parsing and semantic analysis → logical translation → query optimization → evaluation → output

The request is first checked for grammar and meaning, then translated into a logical representation. Optimization selects equivalent operations and physical access methods; evaluation executes that plan and returns the output. Option A follows those roles in order. The other sequences treat DDL and DML language categories as processing stages and place unrelated checks after optimization, so they do not fit.

Evidence in the complete study note

Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.ADB17
DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.ADB17
Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.ADB17

A · correct — This sequence follows checking, representation, strategy selection and execution.

B · incorrect — DDL/DML categories do not form these phases, and checking is misplaced.

C · incorrect — DDL is not a mandatory post-optimization phase of SELECT processing.

D · incorrect — Only option A follows the pipeline, so all sequences are not correct.

Correct answer: D — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability

Page 66 lists atomicity, consistency preservation, isolation, and durability/permanency. Only D preserves all four terms.

Evidence in the complete study note

A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure.
