            Question 149

            T1 reads balance=$500 and adds $100, planning to write $600. T2 reads the same $500, adds $200, and writes $700. T1 then writes $600. What problem occurred?

            • A. Dirty Read
            • B. Lost Update (Write-Write Problem)
            • C. Incorrect Summary Problem
            • D. Deadlock

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 16

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Correct answer: B — Lost update: T1 overwrites T2’s increment with its stale calculation.

            Both transactions read 500. T2 writes 700 after adding 200, but T1 then writes its previously computed 600, erasing T2’s increment. A serial execution would produce 800. This matches the lost-update trace in ADB08; no waiting cycle or aggregate calculation is described, and reading an uncommitted value is not the stated cause.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08
            Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X.ADB13
            Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.ADB08

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Neither transaction is described as reading the other's uncommitted write.

            B · correct — T1's stale write of 600 overwrites T2's added 200; the correct combined result is 800.

            C · incorrect — No aggregate over mutually inconsistent versions is being calculated.

            D · incorrect — No circular waiting or blocked resource requests are present.

            Question 150

            A dirty read occurs when transaction T1 reads data that:

            • A. T1 itself wrote earlier in the same transaction
            • B. T2 modified but has NOT yet committed, and T2 may later abort
            • C. Was permanently deleted from the database
            • D. Was last read more than one hour ago

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 17

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Correct answer: B — Read another transaction’s uncommitted modification.

            ADB08 defines dirty read as consuming a value written by an uncommitted other transaction. If that writer aborts, the dependent read used a value that should not survive. Reading one’s own changes is allowed and is not this anomaly; the age of a value or a completed permanent deletion does not define dirty reading.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08
            A phantom means repeating a predicate query finds a changed qualifying set after another transaction inserts, deletes or changes matching rows.ADB08
            A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90.ADB08

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Reading changes made earlier by the same transaction is not a dirty read.

            B · correct — The read depends on T2's uncommitted update, which may later need undo.

            C · incorrect — Permanent deletion is not the defining uncommitted-value dependency.

            D · incorrect — Elapsed time since a read does not determine whether the writer committed.

            Question 151

            Which lock type allows MULTIPLE transactions to simultaneously READ a data item?

            • A. Exclusive Lock
            • B. Write Lock
            • C. Shared Lock
            • D. Binary Lock

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 18

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB-S04 · Elementary binary locks and shared-lock compatibility

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB-S04 · Elementary binary locks and shared-lock compatibility

            Correct answer: C — Shared lock.

            ADB11 states that a shared lock permits reading and multiple shared holders can coexist on the same item. Exclusive/write locks conflict with another transaction’s shared or exclusive lock on that item. Thus shared locking provides the requested concurrent-reader behavior. A generic binary locked/unlocked label does not establish shared-reader compatibility in the supplied model.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.ADB11
            Shared/exclusive locking adds modes so multiple shared readers can coexist while incompatible exclusive access is excluded.ADB-S04
            One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.ADB11

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — An exclusive lock conflicts with other transactions' read locks on the same item.

            B · incorrect — A write/exclusive lock does not grant multiple independent readers the requested shared ownership.

            C · correct — Shared locks are compatible with other shared locks, permitting multiple readers.

            D · incorrect — The binary label does not provide the explicit S/S compatibility defined in the note.

            Question 152

            In Two-Phase Locking (2PL), a transaction can acquire new locks ONLY during which phase?

            • A. Shrinking Phase
            • B. Termination Phase
            • C. Growing Phase
            • D. Validation Phase

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 19

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Correct answer: C — Growing phase.

            Basic 2PL separates acquiring/upgrading locks from releasing/downgrading them. ADB12 permits acquisition only in the growing phase; after any release, no new lock may be acquired. Termination is a transaction boundary and validation belongs to a different control approach. The growing/shrinking rule is what distinguishes 2PL from unrestricted use of locks.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.ADB12
            Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.ADB12
            Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.ADB16

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — The shrinking phase releases or downgrades locks and forbids new acquisitions.

            B · incorrect — Termination is not the 2PL phase in which new locks are acquired.

            C · correct — Growing permits acquiring and upgrading locks before any release begins.

            D · incorrect — Validation is an optimistic-control stage, not the lock-acquisition phase of 2PL.

            Question 153

            What does Two-Phase Locking (2PL) guarantee that locking alone does NOT guarantee?

            • A. That no deadlocks will occur
            • B. Serializability — results equivalent to some serial execution
            • C. That all transactions complete without aborting
            • D. That every transaction reads the most current data

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 20

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            Correct answer: B — Conflict serializability for well-formed transactions.

            ADB12 explicitly guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed 2PL transactions. Locking without its phase discipline need not provide that ordering guarantee. Basic 2PL can still deadlock and may permit cascading aborts, so it does not guarantee successful completion. Nor does serializability require every read to observe the latest wall-clock update.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.ADB12
            Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.ADB12
            Strict 2PL retains exclusive locks until commit/abort.ADB12

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Basic 2PL can deadlock, so deadlock freedom is not its general guarantee.

            B · correct — The phase discipline guarantees conflict-serializable schedules for well-formed transactions.

            C · incorrect — Deadlock resolution or failures can still abort transactions.

            D · incorrect — Serializability does not require every read to see the newest wall-clock version.

            Question 154

            What is a deadlock in database systems?

            • A. A transaction that executes too slowly
            • B. A circular wait where each transaction holds a resource another needs, and none can proceed
            • C. A type of hardware failure causing data loss
            • D. When a transaction violates the ACID consistency property

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 21

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            Correct answer: B — A circular wait among transactions holding resources needed by others.

            ADB13 defines deadlock through a waiting cycle: each participant holds a resource another needs, so none can advance without an intervention. Slow work alone can still make progress and is not deadlock. Hardware loss and consistency violations are distinct problems that do not require a resource-wait cycle.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13
            A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.ADB13
            Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts.ADB26

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — A slow transaction may still make progress and need not participate in a wait cycle.

            B · correct — Circular hold-and-wait prevents the involved transactions from progressing without intervention.

            C · incorrect — Hardware failure is a different failure category and does not define a lock wait cycle.

            D · incorrect — A consistency violation concerns invalid data states rather than necessarily circular waiting.

            Question 155

            In the Wait-Die deadlock prevention strategy, when a YOUNGER transaction needs a resource held by an OLDER transaction, the younger transaction:

            • A. Wounds (aborts) the older transaction
            • B. Waits for the older transaction to release the resource
            • C. Is immediately aborted and restarted
            • D. Receives the resource immediately due to higher priority

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 22

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Correct answer: C — Abort the younger requester; retry with its original timestamp.

            The requester is younger and the resource holder older. ADB14 says wait–die permits an older requester to wait but aborts a younger requester needing an older holder. C therefore gives the correct action. Restart should retain the original timestamp to improve relative priority; immediately aborted does not require an immediate successful retry or resource grant.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.ADB14

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Wait–die does not let the younger requester abort the older holder.

            B · incorrect — In wait–die, the younger requester dies rather than waiting for the older holder.

            C · correct — The younger requester is aborted and may restart using its original timestamp.

            D · incorrect — The older holder retains priority; the younger requester does not receive the resource immediately.

            Question 156

            In the Wound-Wait strategy, when an OLDER transaction needs a resource held by a YOUNGER transaction:

            • A. The older transaction waits for the younger
            • B. The older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger transaction
            • C. Both transactions are simultaneously aborted
            • D. A deadlock detection algorithm runs

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 23

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Correct answer: B — The older requester aborts the younger holder.

            ADB14 distinguishes wound–wait from wait–die: an older requester wounds the younger holder, while a younger requester waits for an older holder. Here the requester is explicitly older, so B applies. The rule prevents waiting cycles through age-based action; it does not require detecting an existing deadlock first or aborting both participants.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.ADB14
            A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model.ADB13
            A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp.ADB13

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under wound–wait.

            B · correct — The older requester causes the younger resource holder to abort and release its lock.

            C · incorrect — The protocol aborts the younger holder, not both transactions.

            D · incorrect — This is a prevention action based on ages, not a requirement to run cycle detection first.

            Question 157

            Optimistic concurrency control is BEST suited for environments where:

            • A. Transactions frequently write to the same data items
            • B. Write operations always conflict with read operations
            • C. Conflicts between transactions are rare (read-heavy workloads)
            • D. All transactions must complete in strict timestamp order

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 24

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Correct answer: C — Conflicts between transactions are rare (read-heavy workloads)

            Optimistic concurrency control lets transactions read and compute privately, then validates overlapping read/write activity before publishing changes. When conflicts are rare, most work can commit without being discarded. Frequent competing writes or persistent read/write conflicts instead lead to costly retries. Strict timestamp completion describes a separate ordering constraint; it does not supply the low-conflict condition that makes optimistic execution suitable. Read-heavy activity is useful here only insofar as actual conflicts remain uncommon.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries. It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts.ADB16

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Incorrect: frequent competing writes cause validation failures and discarded work.

            B · incorrect — Incorrect: persistent read/write conflicts increase retry costs rather than favoring optimistic execution.

            C · correct — Correct: rare conflicts allow most private work to validate and commit.

            D · incorrect — Incorrect: a required completion order does not imply low contention; optimistic suitability depends on conflicts and retry cost.

            Question 158

            Lock upgrade refers to changing a lock from:

            • A. Exclusive → Shared
            • B. Shared → Exclusive
            • C. No lock → Shared
            • D. Exclusive → No lock

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 25

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Correct answer: B — Shared → Exclusive.

            ADB11 explicitly names S→X an upgrade and X→S a downgrade. The stronger exclusive lock permits writing and can be granted only after conflicting other holders leave. Acquiring a new shared lock is initial acquisition rather than conversion, while releasing an exclusive lock is unlocking. Thus B alone names a lock upgrade.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks. S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave. X→S is a downgrade. The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests. One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.ADB11

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Exclusive-to-shared weakens permissions and is a downgrade.

            B · correct — Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the held lock to permit writing, subject to compatibility.

            C · incorrect — No-lock-to-shared is initial acquisition, not conversion of an already held lock.

            D · incorrect — Exclusive-to-no-lock is release rather than upgrade.

            Question 159

            Which trace demonstrates an incorrect-summary anomaly? The intended anomaly is a mixed-version aggregate, distinct from a nonrepeatable read.

            • A. Two transactions both delete the same record simultaneously
            • B. Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200.
            • C. A transaction reads uncommitted data from another transaction
            • D. A transaction fails to acquire all necessary locks

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 26

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Correct answer: B — B. Initially A=B=100. During T2's transfer of 10 from A to B, T1 sums old A=100 and new B=110, returning 210 although the total-balance invariant is 200.

            The transfer preserves the total balance at 200, but T1 combines the pre-transfer debit balance with the post-transfer credit balance. Its computed 100+110=210 is not a valid summary of a consistent state. This is an incorrect-summary anomaly. Dirty reading is defined by an uncommitted dependency, and lock failure or simultaneous deletion alone does not establish this mixed aggregate.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08
            Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.ADB08
            A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90.ADB08

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Concurrent deletion alone does not specify an inconsistent aggregate.

            B · correct — The mixed old/new balances yield 210 instead of the invariant 200.

            C · incorrect — Reading another transaction's uncommitted value defines a dirty read.

            D · incorrect — Failure to acquire locks concerns scheduling rather than this aggregate result.

            Question 160

            Starvation in a database system occurs when:

            • A. A transaction consumes excessive memory resources
            • B. A transaction is repeatedly bypassed by higher-priority transactions and never executes
            • C. A deadlock persists longer than the timeout period
            • D. The transaction log becomes completely full

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 27

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Correct answer: B — Indefinite postponement while other transactions keep progressing.

            ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without requiring any waiting cycle. Repeatedly favoring higher-priority work can prevent a transaction from executing, matching B. Memory consumption, a full log or a long deadlock are different resource/failure conditions; none alone defines the fairness failure of starvation.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13
            Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle.ADB13
            Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.ADB13

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Excessive memory use is a resource problem rather than the definition of indefinite postponement.

            B · correct — Repeated bypass by other transactions can indefinitely postpone this transaction while work continues.

            C · incorrect — Deadlock requires a waiting cycle; starvation can occur without one.

            D · incorrect — A full log can block work but does not itself define unfair indefinite postponement.

            Question 161

            Which concurrency control technique assigns a unique start-time value to each transaction and uses this to order execution and resolve conflicts?

            • A. Two-Phase Locking
            • B. Shadow Paging
            • C. Timestamp-Based Concurrency Control
            • D. Optimistic Concurrency Control

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 28

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare the transaction timestamp with the item's recorded read and write timestamps.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Correct answer: C — Timestamp-based concurrency control.

            ADB15 assigns TS(T) to each transaction and compares it with item read_TS and write_TS values. Those tests reject operations that would violate timestamp order, so C matches the start-time ordering technique. 2PL orders locking, optimistic control validates private work, and shadow paging is a recovery/storage technique rather than this conflict-ordering protocol.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Assign each transaction TS(T). For item X track read_TS(X), the largest timestamp of a successful reader, and write_TS(X), that of its latest successful writer. A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS. These tests preserve timestamp order.ADB15
            Multiversion control keeps versions so a reader can use an appropriate snapshot.ADB16
            Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers.ADB29

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — 2PL orders lock acquisition and release rather than defining the timestamp validity tests.

            B · incorrect — Shadow paging preserves page versions for recovery rather than ordering concurrent transaction operations by timestamp.

            C · correct — Timestamp ordering compares transaction timestamps with item read/write timestamps to resolve conflicts.

            D · incorrect — Optimistic control validates private read/write work rather than being defined by these timestamp-order tests.

            Question 162

            A well-formed transaction must follow which rule regarding locking?

            • A. Lock all items at the end of the transaction
            • B. Lock a data item BEFORE reading or writing it
            • C. Lock items only when modifying them, not when reading
            • D. Acquire all locks in alphabetical order by item name

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 29

            Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Correct answer: B — Acquire the appropriate lock before accessing the item.

            ADB11 requires ownership of an appropriate lock before access and permits releasing only one’s own locks. Reads therefore need shared or suitable stronger locks in this basic model; writes need exclusive ownership. Alphabetical acquisition may be a separate prevention convention, but it is not the general well-formedness rule and locks cannot be postponed until after access.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.ADB11
            A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks.ADB11
            Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Locking only at the end leaves the earlier accesses unprotected.

            B · correct — A well-formed transaction holds an appropriate lock before reading or writing an item.

            C · incorrect — Basic lock-based access also requires an appropriate read lock, not only locks for writes.

            D · incorrect — A fixed resource order can help prevention, but alphabetical order is not the general well-formedness definition.

            Question 163

            Lock timeout as a deadlock solution works by:

            • A. Detecting cycles in the wait-for graph
            • B. Building a priority queue of all waiting transactions
            • C. Automatically aborting a transaction that has waited too long for a lock
            • D. Locking all required data items before execution begins

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 30

            Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            Correct answer: C — Abort a transaction after its lock wait exceeds the timeout.

            ADB13 describes timeout as aborting long waits, while warning it may mistake slow progress for deadlock. C directly states that mechanism. Detecting cycles is a different method; acquiring all needed locks first is conservative locking; a priority queue alone neither defines a timeout nor guarantees elimination of waiting cycles.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13
            A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.ADB13
            Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.ADB12

            A · incorrect — Cycle detection is graph-based deadlock detection rather than a wait-duration timeout.

            B · incorrect — A priority queue alone does not enforce the stated wait-duration abort policy.

            C · correct — The policy aborts work whose lock wait exceeds the chosen threshold.

            D · incorrect — Obtaining all locks before execution is conservative locking, not timeout handling.

            Question 164

            What are the three phases of query processing in the correct order?

            • A. Optimization, Parsing, Evaluation
            • B. Parsing & Translation, Optimization, Evaluation
            • C. Evaluation, Translation, Optimization
            • D. Parsing, Evaluation, Optimization

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 31

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

            Correct answer: B — Parsing/translation → optimization → evaluation.

            ADB17 checks grammar and semantics, constructs a logical representation, chooses an equivalent efficient execution plan and evaluates it. B groups parsing and translation into the first phase and preserves that dependency order. Plans cannot sensibly be evaluated before construction and selection, and optimization does not precede understanding the query’s syntax and meaning.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.ADB17
            Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.ADB17
            DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.ADB17

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Optimization cannot precede parsing and understanding the query in the stated pipeline.

            B · correct — It preserves analysis/translation, plan optimization and then execution/evaluation.

            C · incorrect — Evaluation cannot be the first phase before the query is represented and planned.

            D · incorrect — It executes before selecting the optimized plan, reversing optimization and evaluation.

            Question 165

            During query translation, SQL is typically converted into which internal representation for processing?

            • A. Machine code instructions
            • B. Binary decision trees
            • C. Relational algebra expressions
            • D. Compressed byte code

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 32

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

            Correct answer: C — Relational algebra expressions or a logical query tree.

            ADB17 states that translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. This allows equivalent rewrites and plan choice before physical execution. Machine code or bytecode may appear in particular execution implementations, but they are not the general logical translation target asked for here; a binary decision tree is also not the defined representation.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.ADB17
            A query tree has base relations at leaves and operators at internal nodes; a query graph emphasizes relations and predicates.ADB17
            A physical execution plan adds scan/index choices and algorithms.ADB17

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Machine code is not the logical relational representation described for query translation.

            B · incorrect — A binary decision tree is not the note's general query-algebra representation.

            C · correct — Relational algebra expresses the logical operators that can be rewritten and optimized.

            D · incorrect — Compressed bytecode is not the stated general logical query representation.

            Question 166

            The query optimizer's primary goal is to:

            • A. Ensure queries return results in sorted order
            • B. Find an execution plan that minimizes the overall cost of retrieving data
            • C. Maximize the number of indexes used in the query
            • D. Ensure all tables are accessed in the order written in SQL

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 33

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

            ADB23 · Indexes, statistics and re-optimization

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            ADB18 · Heuristic and semantic query rewrites

            ADB23 · Indexes, statistics and re-optimization

            Correct answer: B — Choose a low-cost equivalent execution plan.

            ADB19 estimates resource costs such as I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and communication for candidate plans. Optimization compares equivalent ways to return the same result and chooses a suitable low-cost strategy. It does not seek index count, force textual table order or impose sorting that the query never requested. The estimate need not prove a global real-world minimum.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions. Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows. For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger. Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero. Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches.ADB19
            Avoid universal rules that joins always beat subqueries, functions can never use indexes or more indexes always improve performance.ADB23
            Cost-based optimization estimates candidate plans instead of relying on rules alone.ADB18

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Sorting is required only when query semantics need it, not as the universal optimizer goal.

            B · correct — The optimizer seeks an efficient equivalent plan under the selected resource-cost model.

            C · incorrect — More indexes used does not necessarily mean lower cost or better execution.

            D · incorrect — Equivalent join reordering can reduce cost; SQL textual order need not dictate access order.

            Question 167

            In the textbook local rotating-disk cost model, data is not memory-resident and query execution is disk-bound; client/network and CPU costs are negligible by comparison. Which component dominates the estimated query cost?

            • A. CPU processing time
            • B. Disk I/O time (seek time + transfer time)
            • C. Memory allocation overhead
            • D. Network latency to the client

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 34

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Correct answer: B — B. Disk I/O time (seek time + transfer time)

            The specified disk-bound model estimates the cost of seeks and transferred blocks. Because CPU, memory-management and network costs are negligible by assumption, disk I/O dominates this query's estimated cost. This is a contextual model rather than a universal fact about all databases: memory-resident or distributed workloads can have different dominant resources. The answer follows the scenario's stated objective.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.ADB19

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — CPU cost is negligible in the specified model.

            B · correct — Seek and transfer time dominate the stated disk-bound workload.

            C · incorrect — Memory-management overhead is negligible here.

            D · incorrect — Client/network cost is negligible in this local scenario.

            Question 168

            In the disk I/O cost formula Cost = (S x tS) + (B x tT), what does 'B' represent?

            • A. Block size in bytes
            • B. Number of disk blocks transferred
            • C. Buffer pool size
            • D. Binary search operations

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 35

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Correct answer: B — The number of transferred disk blocks.

            ADB19 computes disk cost as seeks times seek duration plus transferred blocks times per-block transfer time. Therefore B in the formula is a block count, making B×tT the total transfer time. Block size, buffer capacity and search-operation count are different quantities and would not have the units required by this expression.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.ADB19

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Block size is bytes per block rather than the number multiplied by per-block transfer time.

            B · correct — B counts transferred blocks, so B×tT gives their total transfer time.

            C · incorrect — Buffer-pool capacity is not the transferred-block count in this formula.

            D · incorrect — Binary-search operation count is not the disk-block transfer term.

            Question 169

            The UNDO operation in database recovery is used to:

            • A. Re-apply changes of committed transactions not yet written to disk
            • B. Create new checkpoint entries in the log
            • C. Reverse changes made by incomplete or aborted transactions
            • D. Transfer data from cache to permanent disk storage

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 36

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB07 · Read/write operations, buffers and log records

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB07 · Read/write operations, buffers and log records

            Correct answer: C — Reverse incomplete or aborted transaction effects.

            ADB27 uses undo to restore before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing a transaction’s updates backward. This removes changes that must not survive. Reapplying committed changes is redo, checkpoint records bound recovery searches, and transferring dirty buffers to storage is page flushing. Only C describes undo rather than another recovery or storage operation.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.ADB27
            A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.ADB30
            In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo.ADB30

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Reapplying missing committed updates is redo rather than undo.

            B · incorrect — Checkpoint creation records recovery state and is not reversal of incomplete effects.

            C · correct — Undo restores old values to remove incomplete or aborted transaction changes.

            D · incorrect — Writing a buffer to disk is flushing rather than restoring before-images.

            Question 170

            The REDO operation in database recovery is used to:

            • A. Abort all active transactions found in the log
            • B. Reverse changes made by failed transactions
            • C. Re-apply changes of committed transactions not yet written to disk
            • D. Create shadow copies of database pages

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 37

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Correct answer: C — Reapply required logged after-images, including committed changes missing from pages.

            ADB27 describes redo as installing logged after-images when necessary. In the simple teaching model it preserves committed work not yet on disk, matching C. ARIES may repeat history more broadly before loser undo, so C describes the ordinary purpose rather than every algorithm’s full phase. Aborting transactions and reversing failed changes are different actions.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.ADB27
            Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.ADB29
            Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable.ADB29

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Aborting active transactions is not the operation of applying logged after-images.

            B · incorrect — Reversing incomplete effects is undo rather than redo.

            C · correct — Redo can restore committed changes whose data pages were not durable at the crash.

            D · incorrect — Shadow-page creation is a separate copy-on-write technique rather than logged redo.

            Question 171

            What is the fundamental durable-write ordering rule of write-ahead logging? In B, 'actual data changes' means writing the corresponding changed data page to persistent storage, not modifying a volatile buffer.

            • A. Write data to disk before creating the log record
            • B. Log records must be written to stable storage BEFORE making the actual data changes
            • C. All transactions must commit before any log entries are written
            • D. Log records are written only after a system crash occurs

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 38

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Correct answer: B — B. Log records must be written to stable storage BEFORE making the actual data changes

            WAL requires the recovery log for an update to reach stable storage before its corresponding changed page is written to disk. A volatile buffer may already contain the change, so this rule does not order every CPU assignment after a log flush. A reverses the required durable order; C and D postpone logs until too late to support recovery of earlier persistent changes.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.ADB27
            Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not.ADB27
            Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.ADB27

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Data-before-log reverses WAL's required durable ordering.

            B · correct — With the defined durable-write scope, the log reaches stable storage first.

            C · incorrect — Update logs may need to be durable before commit and before data flushing.

            D · incorrect — Recovery requires logs that were durable before the crash.

            Question 172

            In a simple quiescent checkpoint exercise, all transactions have completed and the required log/data pages are flushed at the checkpoint. How does that checkpoint reduce later recovery search work?

            • A. Preventing all types of hardware failures
            • B. Encrypting log records for faster access
            • C. Providing a known consistent state so recovery can start from there instead of the log beginning
            • D. Automatically committing all active transactions periodically

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 39

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            Correct answer: C — C. Providing a known consistent state so recovery can start from there instead of the log beginning

            The quiescent checkpoint supplies a durable boundary for the simplified exercise. With no active transaction spanning it and the required pages flushed, recovery need not scan all earlier history to redo those completed changes. C captures that bounded search. Checkpointing does not prevent hardware failure, gain its benefit from encryption or automatically commit active transactions. Fuzzy checkpoints require different starting-point qualifications.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.ADB30
            Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.ADB30
            A checkpoint is neither a full backup nor an automatic commit of active transactions.ADB30

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Recording recovery state does not prevent hardware failures.

            B · incorrect — Encryption is not the mechanism reducing log-search work.

            C · correct — The specified durable checkpoint bounds the history needed in this exercise.

            D · incorrect — Transactions have completed here; a checkpoint does not automatically commit active work.

            Question 173

            In deferred update (No-Undo) recovery, actual database modifications are written to disk:

            • A. Immediately as each SQL statement executes
            • B. Only AFTER the transaction successfully commits
            • C. When a checkpoint operation is triggered
            • D. At regular 5-minute intervals regardless of transaction state

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 40

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Correct answer: B — After successful commit, in the deferred-update model.

            ADB29 keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database. Only committed effects may therefore be installed in its actual database pages, which is the property B expresses. This does not require every committed page to be flushed immediately. Checkpoints and periodic timers cannot independently authorize writing uncommitted changes while retaining the claimed No-Undo model.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.ADB29
            Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.ADB29
            Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable.ADB29

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Immediate per-statement persistent writes can expose uncommitted effects and do not define deferred update.

            B · correct — The model does not install uncommitted effects in the persistent database; committed changes can be written later.

            C · incorrect — A checkpoint alone does not make an uncommitted transaction eligible for persistent installation.

            D · incorrect — A fixed timer cannot ignore transaction commit status while preserving deferred-update semantics.

            Question 174

            Shadow paging recovery technique preserves the original database pages by:

            • A. Creating a backup on a separate server
            • B. Writing all modifications to NEW shadow pages, keeping originals intact until commit
            • C. Encrypting pages before any modification
            • D. Storing pages in sorted order for faster access

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 41

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            Correct answer: B — Write changed data to new pages while preserving the committed page map.

            ADB29 preserves the committed version and writes changed data at new locations. Shadow paging keeps the old page map plus a modified map; commit atomically installs the new durable root after needed pages are durable. B captures the copy-on-write preservation, although the unchanged old map is the shadow rather than the name of each newly modified page.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            In-place update overwrites the original location. Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version. Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable. Before commit, a crash uses the old map. It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.ADB29
            A full backup copies the database to separate storage; scheduled backups plus archived logs support restoration to a chosen recoverable point.ADB26
            Rollback handles failed/uncommitted work; redo preserves committed work missing from pages; checkpoints reduce log-search work; backups provide another stored copy.ADB26

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — A separate-server backup is not the page-map copy-on-write mechanism of shadow paging.

            B · correct — Changes use new pages, preserving the originals until the new committed map is safely installed.

            C · incorrect — Encryption does not preserve the old page mapping or provide the stated rollback mechanism.

            D · incorrect — Sorting pages is an access-layout choice rather than preserving committed copies.

            Question 175

            Which type of database failure is caused by accidental deletion of important data by a user?

            • A. Hardware failure
            • B. Natural disaster
            • C. Software error
            • D. Human error

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 42

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB-S05 · Classify a failure by its stated cause

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB-S05 · Classify a failure by its stated cause

            Correct answer: D — Human error.

            The described cause is an accidental user action, not faulty hardware, a natural event or a software defect. ADB26 treats human mistakes separately and notes they may need point-in-time restoration before a bad committed operation. Ordinary crash redo would otherwise preserve a committed deletion rather than recognize the user’s intention.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts. Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure. A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive. Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs. Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.ADB26
            An accidental user deletion is human error even if the software executes the requested command correctly.ADB-S05
            A software failure originates in erroneous program behavior, such as a logical programming defect, invalid operation or operating-system fault.ADB-S05

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — No hardware malfunction is stated; the cause is the user's mistaken deletion.

            B · incorrect — A natural disaster is not the cause described in the prompt.

            C · incorrect — The software may have executed the requested deletion correctly; the stated mistake belongs to the user.

            D · correct — Accidental deletion by a user is a human error.

ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.ADB27

            Question 177

            Which type of distributed database uses the SAME DBMS software at every site?

            • A. Heterogeneous distributed database
            • B. Homogeneous distributed database
            • C. Middleware-based database
            • D. Partially replicated database

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 44

            Separate coordinated network placement from engine compatibility and semantic integration.

            ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Study-guide references

            ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Correct answer: B — Homogeneous distributed database.

            ADB33 identifies homogeneous systems by compatible DBMS technology across sites. Using the same DBMS software fits that classification. Heterogeneous systems integrate differing engines, models or interfaces. Middleware describes integration architecture and partial replication describes placement of copies, so neither substitutes for the homogeneity classification asked for here.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A distributed database contains logically related data across networked sites, managed as a coordinated system. A homogeneous system uses compatible DBMS technology across sites; a heterogeneous system integrates differing DBMSs, data models, schemas or interfaces. Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction. Same DBMS does not imply identical local schemas, automatic replication or immediate synchronization.ADB33
            Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.ADB37

            D · incorrect — Partial replication describes where selected copies reside rather than which DBMS software sites use.

            Question 178

            Horizontal fragmentation divides a table based on:

            • A. Splitting columns into separate subsets
            • B. Splitting rows into subsets based on a condition
            • C. Combining two tables into one larger table
            • D. Replicating the table to multiple sites

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Correct answer: B — Split rows by predicates.

            ADB36 defines horizontal fragmentation as selecting row subsets using predicates and reconstructing the relation by union. Column subsets belong to vertical fragmentation. Combining tables is not fragmentation, and copying a whole table is replication. Thus B identifies both the item being split and the rule used to decide fragment membership.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
            Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once.ADB37
            Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.ADB37

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Column splitting is vertical fragmentation rather than horizontal fragmentation.

            B · correct — Horizontal fragments contain rows selected by stated predicates.

            C · incorrect — Combining tables increases the combined relation rather than splitting one table into row subsets.

            D · incorrect — Replicating copies preserves the whole table at more sites rather than partitioning its rows.

            Question 179

            In vertical fragmentation, why must the PRIMARY KEY be included in every fragment?

            • A. To speed up INSERT operations
            • B. To prevent duplicate rows
            • C. To enable reconstruction of the original table by joining fragments on the primary key
            • D. To ensure proper replication across sites

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            Correct answer: C — A repeated key or row identifier lets vertical pieces join back losslessly.

            ADB36 repeats a key or row identifier across vertical fragments so attributes from the same original row can be matched during reconstruction. C states that purpose. The general requirement is a suitable identifier, not necessarily the particular declared primary key if another row identifier is used. It is unrelated to mandatory replication or inherently faster inserts.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
            Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.ADB36
            Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.ADB36
