            D · incorrect — Replication copies data and is distinct from reconstructing vertical column fragments.

            Question 180

            Which data replication scheme stores each data fragment at ONLY ONE site with NO copies?

            • A. Full replication
            • B. Partial replication
            • C. No replication (non-redundant allocation)
            • D. Hybrid replication

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 47

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Correct answer: C — No replication, or nonredundant allocation.

            ADB37 explicitly calls storing each fragment once nonredundant allocation. Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site, while partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites. A hybrid can mix strategies, but the stem specifies exactly one location and no copies for every fragment, so C is the precise classification.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.ADB37
            Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.ADB37
            Snapshot replication transfers a copy at intervals; incremental replication transfers changes.ADB37

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Full replication stores copies throughout the relevant sites rather than one copy per fragment.

            B · incorrect — Partial replication still copies selected fragments and therefore does not mean no copies.

            C · correct — Nonredundant allocation stores each fragment at one site without replicas.

            D · incorrect — A hybrid can combine policies, but the stated universal no-copy arrangement is specifically nonreplicated.

            Question 181

            Transparency in distributed databases means that:

            • A. All data is encrypted and transparent to hackers
            • B. The distribution complexity is hidden from users who interact as if using a single database
            • C. Users can see all technical details of how data is distributed
            • D. All sites must use the same operating system

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 48

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

            Correct answer: B — Hide distribution details behind a single logical database experience.

            ADB35 defines transparency through which distribution details are hidden: sites, fragment reconstruction or replica selection/maintenance. Together these can let clients work with a single logical database abstraction. B captures that broad meaning. Transparency is not encryption, disclosure of every technical detail or a requirement that operating systems be identical.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Location transparency hides which site holds a named object. Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation. Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained. The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three.ADB35
            Different operating systems are possible but do not define the distinction.ADB33
            Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions.ADB24

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Encryption protects content; transparency here concerns hiding distribution complexity from legitimate users.

            B · correct — Distribution details can be hidden so users work with one logical database abstraction.

            C · incorrect — Transparency hides selected implementation details rather than exposing all of them.

            D · incorrect — Operating-system uniformity does not define distribution transparency.

            Question 182

            Hybrid fragmentation combines which two fragmentation types?

            • A. Replication and Partitioning
            • B. Horizontal and Vertical fragmentation
            • C. Client-Server and Middleware architectures
            • D. Homogeneous and Heterogeneous distribution

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 49

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            ADB33 · Distributed, homogeneous and heterogeneous systems

            Correct answer: B — Horizontal and vertical fragmentation.

            ADB36 defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in a suitable order. Reconstructing reverses those operations using unions for horizontal pieces and key joins for corresponding vertical pieces. Replication, deployment architectures and DBMS homogeneity are different design dimensions rather than the two fragmentation types combined by hybrid fragmentation.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
            Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.ADB36
            Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.ADB36

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Replication copies data and is not the second fragmentation dimension in the hybrid definition.

            B · correct — Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row splits with vertical column splits.

            C · incorrect — Client-server and middleware classify architectures rather than fragmentation operations.

            D · incorrect — Homogeneous/heterogeneous classifies system technology compatibility rather than row/column splitting.

            Question 183

            With full replication and synchronous propagation before acknowledgment, which listed disadvantage specifically concerns maintaining copies during an update-heavy workload? Assume usable replicas can serve reads.

            • A. Data becomes unavailable when any site fails
            • B. Updates incur propagation and coordination overhead because changes must reach the required copies before acknowledgment.
            • C. It requires all sites to use the same DBMS software
            • D. Queries can only be answered from the primary site

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 50

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Correct answer: B — B. Updates incur propagation and coordination overhead because changes must reach the required copies before acknowledgment.

            Full replication stores the entire database at each relevant site, so updates create propagation and coordination work. The stated synchronous policy places that work before acknowledgment, adding update latency in the update-heavy scenario. This is the disadvantage described by B. Usable copies can serve reads and improve availability; full replication neither implies identical DBMS software nor restricts queries to one primary site.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.ADB37
            Eager/synchronous replication coordinates propagation before the specified commit/acknowledgment point, increasing update latency.ADB37
            Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.ADB37

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Usable replicas can keep data available after one site fails.

            B · correct — The stated synchronous policy adds propagation and coordination work before acknowledgment.

            C · incorrect — Full replication is a copy-placement policy, not a requirement to standardize every DBMS.

            D · incorrect — Usable replicas can serve reads in the stated scenario.

            Question 184

            What does ACID stand for in database transactions?

            • A. Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Durability
            • B. Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
            • C. Availability, Consistency, Integrity, Durability
            • D. Atomicity, Correctness, Isolation, Distribution

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 1

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Correct answer: B — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

            ADB06 gives all-or-none effects, preservation of declared rules, controlled interference and persistence after failure as the four ACID properties. B names them correctly. The other options substitute concurrency, availability, integrity, correctness or distribution for the defined terms, changing the acronym rather than describing an equivalent expansion.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.ADB06

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Concurrency incorrectly replaces Consistency in the acronym.

            B · correct — The expansion exactly matches the four ACID property names.

            C · incorrect — Availability and Integrity replace Atomicity and Isolation, which are the defined terms.

            D · incorrect — Correctness and Distribution do not replace Consistency and Durability in ACID.

            Question 185

            Which ACID property ensures that either ALL operations of a transaction complete or NONE do?

            • A. Consistency
            • B. Isolation
            • C. Atomicity
            • D. Durability

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 2

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Correct answer: C — Atomicity.

            The requested property concerns whether partial transaction effects can survive. ADB06 assigns all-or-none application to atomicity. A correct transaction also preserves consistency, concurrency needs isolation and completed commits need durability, but those are different guarantees. C is therefore the property matching the explicit ALL or NONE condition.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.ADB06

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Consistency concerns preservation of integrity rules rather than the indivisible effect boundary itself.

            B · incorrect — Isolation governs concurrent interference rather than all-or-none transaction effects.

            C · correct — Atomicity makes the transaction effects succeed together or be removed together.

            D · incorrect — Durability protects committed effects rather than defining partial-success handling.

            Question 186

            If A=5000 and B=8000, and 750 is transferred from A to B, what values satisfy the Consistency property?

            • A. A=4250, B=8750, sum=13000
            • B. A=4250, B=8000, sum=12250
            • C. A=5000, B=8750, sum=13750
            • D. A=5000, B=8000, sum=13000

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 3

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Correct answer: A — A=4250, B=8750, total=13000.

            Subtracting 750 from A gives 4250 and adding it to B gives 8750; their total remains 13000. A implements both the specified operation and its total-balance invariant. B and C apply only one side. D preserves the initial total but does not perform the requested transfer, so invariant preservation alone does not make it the successful-transfer result.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.ADB06
            Unchanged or reverse-transfer balances can also preserve that sum; only the requested debit/credit implements the specified successful transfer.ADB06
            Both balances total 13,000.ADB06

            Choice by choice

            A · correct — It performs the 750 debit and credit and preserves the total of 13000.

            B · incorrect — The debit occurs without its credit, reducing the total to 12250.

            C · incorrect — The credit occurs without its debit, increasing the total to 13750.

            D · incorrect — It preserves the starting total but leaves both accounts unchanged rather than performing the transfer.

            Question 187

            Which ACID property ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other?

            • A. Atomicity
            • B. Durability
            • C. Consistency
            • D. Isolation

            Study-guide sections

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Correct answer: D — Isolation.

            ADB06 assigns concurrent-interference control to isolation. That is the distinguishing phrase in the stem. Atomicity handles partial effects, durability handles committed persistence, and consistency means correct work preserves declared rules. Different isolation levels provide different detailed guarantees, so this classification does not imply that all implementations offer serializability by default.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.ADB06

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Atomicity governs partial effects within a transaction rather than concurrent interference.

            B · incorrect — Durability concerns persistence of committed changes after failures.

            C · incorrect — Consistency concerns declared integrity rules under correct business logic.

            D · correct — Isolation controls interference among concurrently executing transactions.

            Question 188

            Which ACID property guarantees committed changes survive system crashes?

            • A. Atomicity
            • B. Consistency
            • C. Isolation
            • D. Durability

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 5

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Correct answer: D — Durability.

            ADB06 defines durability by persistence of committed effects despite failure. Recovery information can provide this even when changed data pages were buffered at the instant of commit. All-or-none application, invariant preservation and concurrent isolation serve different transaction guarantees, so only durability matches survival of successful commits after a crash.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A transaction is a logical unit of database work, including read-only work. Atomicity means all effects or none; consistency means correct work preserves integrity rules; isolation controls concurrent interference; durability preserves committed effects despite failure. A DBMS cannot automatically make incorrect business logic consistent.ADB06

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Atomicity concerns all-or-none application rather than the persistence of completed commits.

            B · incorrect — Consistency concerns validity of declared invariants rather than crash survival of commits.

            C · incorrect — Isolation controls concurrent interactions rather than persistence after a crash.

            D · correct — Durability preserves committed effects across system failures.

            Question 189

            A transaction that has executed all operations but NOT YET committed is in which state?

            • A. Active
            • B. Partially Committed
            • C. Committed
            • D. Failed

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 6

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Correct answer: B — Partially committed.

            ADB06 places a transaction in Partially committed after its last operation finishes but before durable commitment is assured. The stem states exactly that boundary. Active means operations are still executing; Committed needs successful commit; Failed needs an error. Finishing the operation list alone does not establish the committed state.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Active means operations are executing. Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. Committed means commitment succeeded. A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt. Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability. Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions.ADB06

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Active describes ongoing operation execution, not the interval after the last operation finishes.

            B · correct — The last operation finished, but commitment is not yet assured.

            C · incorrect — The stem explicitly says the transaction has not yet committed.

            D · incorrect — No execution or commit failure is reported.

            Question 190

            In the Aborted state, what happens to all changes made by the transaction?

            • A. Changes are permanently saved
            • B. All changes are rolled back restoring the database to its pre-transaction state
            • C. The transaction waits for resources
            • D. The transaction restarts automatically

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 7

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the transaction's guarantee or lifecycle boundary described by the scenario.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Correct answer: B — Its effects have been rolled back; other committed transactions remain.

            ADB06 reaches Aborted after rollback. Thus the aborted transaction’s own changes are removed rather than permanently saved. Restoring pre-transaction state must be understood relative to its effects, not erasing unrelated concurrent commits. A restart can be a new attempt, but is not automatic merely because the aborted state was reached.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Active means operations are executing. Partially committed means the last operation finished but durable commitment is not yet assured. Committed means commitment succeeded. A failure leads to Failed, then Aborted after rollback; a transaction may terminate or be restarted as a new attempt. Concurrency control primarily enforces isolation; recovery supports atomicity and durability. Transaction management is the broader subsystem, so both it and recovery management can be legitimate answers to broad responsibility questions.ADB06
            Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward.ADB27
            Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk.ADB27

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Permanent saving is a committed outcome, not an aborted outcome.

            B · correct — Rollback removes this transaction's effects while retaining other transactions' legitimate committed work.

            C · incorrect — Waiting for a lock describes a blocked executing transaction rather than completed rollback.

            D · incorrect — An aborted transaction may be retried, but automatic restart is not guaranteed.

            Question 191

            Which log record signals successful completion of transaction T?

            • A. [start_transaction, T]
            • B. [abort, T]
            • C. [write_item, T, X, old, new]
            • D. [commit, T]

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 8

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB07 · Read/write operations, buffers and log records

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB07 · Read/write operations, buffers and log records

            Correct answer: D — [commit, T].

            ADB07 identifies COMMIT as the record of successful transaction completion. START begins work, UPDATE records a data change and ABORT marks failed termination/rollback handling. A data write by itself does not prove the enclosing transaction committed, and an abort record can begin rollback rather than confirm it has completed.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A conceptual log can contain START, UPDATE(T,X,old,new), COMMIT, ABORT and END records. Before-images support undo; after-images support redo. Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read. COMMIT records successful completion; an ABORT record can mark the start of rollback rather than prove every undo step is complete.ADB07

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — The start record indicates beginning work rather than successful completion.

            B · incorrect — Abort records failure/rollback handling instead of successful commitment.

            C · incorrect — An update record describes one changed item, not successful transaction completion.

            D · correct — The commit record signals successful completion of transaction T.

            Question 192

            The Read_item(X) command transfers data in which order?

            • A. Disk -> Program variable -> Buffer
            • B. Buffer -> Disk -> Program variable
            • C. Disk -> Buffer -> Program variable
            • D. Program variable -> Buffer -> Disk

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 9

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Trace movement between program variables, buffers and disk, or the meaning of a recorded transaction event.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB07 · Read/write operations, buffers and log records

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB07 · Read/write operations, buffers and log records

            Correct answer: C — Disk page → buffer → program variable.

            ADB07 locates X’s page, loads it into a buffer if absent and copies the item from that buffer into the program variable. C gives that conceptual data movement order. A cached page may avoid the physical disk read, but the program still reads through the buffer. The reverse direction describes a write path rather than read_item.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            read_item(X) locates X's page, brings it into a buffer if absent, and copies X into a program variable. write_item(X) copies the new program value into the buffered page, marking it dirty. Writing that page to disk can occur later according to the buffer policy; write_item is not inherently an immediate disk flush. Insert and delete also modify data; sorting is a query-processing operation rather than a primitive item update.ADB07
            Real systems may use physical or logical records, and need not log every read.ADB07
            Before-images support undo; after-images support redo.ADB07

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — The page is buffered before the item is copied to the program variable.

            B · incorrect — A read does not first send the buffer to disk before obtaining the variable value.

            C · correct — The page enters the buffer if needed, then its item is copied into the program variable.

            D · incorrect — Program-variable-to-buffer-to-disk describes writing, not reading into a variable.

            Question 193

            In a multi-user system, which mechanisms does the DBMS use to manage concurrent access?

            • A. Only backup systems
            • B. Locks, timestamps, and scheduling algorithms
            • C. Physical user separation
            • D. Only file system permissions

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 10

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            Correct answer: B — Locks, timestamp rules and transaction scheduling.

            ADB11 defines compatible shared/exclusive locks and ADB15 orders conflicting operations with timestamp tests. These are actual concurrency-control mechanisms that constrain transaction schedules. Backups provide copies for recovery, and file permissions determine access rather than safe interleavings. Physical separation of people also does not coordinate their concurrent database operations.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.ADB11
            Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts.ADB26
            Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes.ADB09

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Backups support restoration rather than scheduling safe concurrent reads and writes.

            B · correct — Locks and timestamp rules control conflicting accesses and permissible schedules.

            C · incorrect — Separating users physically does not coordinate their concurrent operations on shared database items.

            D · incorrect — File permissions alone do not enforce isolation among authorized concurrent transactions.

            Question 194

            The Lost Update problem is also called:

            • A. Read-Read Problem
            • B. Write-Write Problem
            • C. Read-Write Problem
            • D. Phantom Read Problem

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 11

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Correct answer: B — Write-write problem, as shorthand for a lost-update overwrite.

            ADB08 illustrates both transactions reading 500, one writing 700 and the other later overwriting it with stale 600. The conflict is between their writes, which explains the offered write-write shorthand. This is not a claim that every pair of writes loses an update: the stale calculation and overwrite are essential. Read/read and phantom behavior describe different situations.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Two reads alone do not overwrite and lose an update.

            B · correct — The stale write overwrites another write, motivating this write-write shorthand.

            C · incorrect — The defining loss is the later stale overwrite, not merely an arbitrary read/write pair.

            D · incorrect — A phantom changes a predicate query's qualifying row set rather than overwriting one balance.

            Question 195

            • B. A transaction reads data modified by another uncommitted transaction

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Correct answer: B — Reading another transaction’s uncommitted data.

            ADB08 defines dirty read through another transaction’s uncommitted write. The value can disappear if its writer aborts, leaving dependent work based on invalid data. Reading committed data or two readers accessing one item is not inherently dirty. Invalid-format writes concern data validity rather than whether the read-from transaction has committed.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08

            A · incorrect — Reading only committed values avoids the defining uncommitted-writer dependency.

            Question 196

            Which trace demonstrates an incorrect-summary anomaly, meaning an aggregate that mixes mutually inconsistent versions? Treat nonrepeatable read as a separate anomaly.

            • A. A transaction reads data after another commits
            • B. Initially A=B=100. T2 transfers 10 from A to B while T1 reads old A=100 and new B=110, reporting 210 rather than the invariant total 200.
            • C. Two transactions delete the same record
            • D. A transaction reads its own uncommitted data

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 13

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Trace which transaction wrote each value and whether an overwrite or mixed-version read occurs.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB08 · Diagnose concurrency anomalies from a trace

            Correct answer: B — B. Initially A=B=100. T2 transfers 10 from A to B while T1 reads old A=100 and new B=110, reporting 210 rather than the invariant total 200.

            The transfer subtracts and adds the same amount, preserving a total of 200. T1 instead adds an old A balance to a new B balance and obtains 210, combining versions that do not form a consistent summary. That is the incorrect-summary anomaly. Reading committed data, deleting a record or reading one's own uncommitted changes alone does not establish this aggregate defect.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Lost update: T1 and T2 both read 500; T2 adds 200 and writes 700; T1 adds 100 to its stale value and writes 600. Correct serial execution yields 800. Dirty read: T2 reads a value written by uncommitted T1; if T1 aborts, dependent work must be reconsidered. Reading one's own changes is not a dirty read.ADB08
            Incorrect summary mixes mutually inconsistent versions: a transfer moves 10 from A=100 to B=100; a sum reading old A=100 and new B=110 gets 210 instead of the invariant 200.ADB08
            A single committed update from B=20 to B=50 does not alone prove an invalid summary of 90.ADB08

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — A read after another commit is not by itself an inconsistent aggregate.

            B · correct — 100+110=210 mixes versions and violates the preserved total 200.

            C · incorrect — Concurrent deletions alone do not show this summary anomaly.

            D · incorrect — Reading one's own changes is not the stated mixed-version aggregate.

            Question 197

            A Shared Lock allows:

            • A. Only one transaction to read an item
            • B. Multiple transactions to read simultaneously but not write
            • C. One transaction to read and write exclusively
            • D. Multiple transactions to write simultaneously

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 14

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Correct answer: B — Compatible readers, with no writing under a shared lock.

            ADB11 permits multiple shared locks on one item, each for reading. Writing requires a suitable exclusive lock, which conflicts with other shared holders. Thus B describes shared-lock behavior in the basic lock-based model. Exclusive read/write ownership and multiple simultaneous writers are not shared locking; multiversion snapshot rules are a separate model.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.ADB11
            One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.ADB11
            No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.ADB11

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — More than one transaction may hold compatible shared read locks on the same item.

            B · correct — Shared locks permit multiple readers but do not authorize writes under that lock mode.

            C · incorrect — Sole read/write ownership describes an exclusive lock.

            D · incorrect — Shared locks do not allow multiple transactions to write simultaneously.

            Question 198

            An Exclusive Lock allows:

            • A. Multiple transactions to read concurrently
            • B. Multiple transactions to write simultaneously
            • C. Only one transaction to both read and write, blocking all other access
            • D. Multiple readers and one writer simultaneously

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 15

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Correct answer: C — The exclusive holder may read and write; conflicting access to that item is blocked.

            ADB11 permits an exclusive lock holder to read and write and makes that item’s X lock conflict with another S or X. C is correct in this basic model. Blocking all other access means conflicting access to the same item, not the entire database; locks on other items remain independent and multiversion systems can have additional snapshot-reader behavior.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A shared (S) lock permits reading; multiple S locks on the same item can coexist. An exclusive (X) lock permits its holder to read and write and conflicts with another S or X on that item. Locks on different items do not conflict merely because one is exclusive. These are the basic lock-based rules; multiversion systems can permit additional snapshot-reader behavior.ADB11
            One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy.ADB11
            S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave.ADB11

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Other transactions' shared reads conflict with an exclusive lock on the same item in this model.

            B · incorrect — Two exclusive writers cannot hold compatible locks on the same item.

            C · correct — One holder can read/write the locked item while incompatible same-item accesses wait or abort.

            D · incorrect — Concurrent same-item shared readers conflict with this exclusive writer under the basic rules.

            Question 199

            In Two-Phase Locking (2PL), during the Growing Phase a transaction:

            • A. Releases locks only
            • B. Acquires locks without releasing any
            • C. Acquires and releases locks freely
            • D. Makes no lock requests

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 16

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            Correct answer: B — Acquire or upgrade locks without releasing them.

            ADB12 defines growing as the acquisition/upgrade phase and shrinking as the release/downgrade phase. Once any lock is released, no further acquisition is allowed. B therefore matches growing. Freely mixing acquisition and release would abandon the two-phase discipline that guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.ADB12
            Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.ADB12
            Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.ADB12

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Releasing locks belongs to shrinking rather than growing.

            B · correct — Growing acquires or upgrades locks before any release occurs.

            C · incorrect — Freely acquiring after release violates the defining 2PL phase restriction.

            D · incorrect — Growing is precisely the phase in which lock requests may be made.

            Question 200

            Which concurrency control technique uses start-times to order transaction execution?

            • A. Locking
            • B. Optimistic Concurrency Control
            • C. Timestamp-based Concurrency Control
            • D. Shadow Paging

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 17

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare the transaction timestamp with the item's recorded read and write timestamps.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Correct answer: C — Timestamp-based concurrency control.

            ADB15 assigns each transaction a timestamp and checks reads and writes against item read/write timestamps. These checks preserve timestamp order and can abort stale operations. Locking instead uses ownership compatibility, optimistic control validates private work and shadow paging concerns recovery page maps. Only C names the start-time ordering technique described.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Assign each transaction TS(T). For item X track read_TS(X), the largest timestamp of a successful reader, and write_TS(X), that of its latest successful writer. A read by T aborts if TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and updates read_TS. A write aborts if TS(T)<read_TS(X) or TS(T)<write_TS(X); otherwise it succeeds and sets write_TS. These tests preserve timestamp order.ADB15
            Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.ADB16
            Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.ADB29

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Locking uses lock compatibility and protocols rather than being defined by transaction start-time ordering.

            B · incorrect — Optimistic control validates private read/write sets rather than applying these timestamp-order tests.

            C · correct — Timestamp-based control orders valid conflicting operations using transaction timestamps.

            D · incorrect — Shadow paging preserves committed page maps for recovery rather than ordering concurrent operations.

            Question 201

            Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is best suited for:

            • A. High-conflict write-heavy workloads
            • B. Read-heavy workloads where conflicts are rare
            • C. Single-user database systems
            • D. Distributed transactions only

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 18

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Consider conflicts, private work and validation costs, or lock-management overhead.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Correct answer: B — Read-heavy, low-conflict workloads.

            ADB16 computes privately, validates and publishes, retrying failed validation. Low-conflict workloads let most work succeed; high write contention wastes computation on aborts. B states that criterion explicitly. Single-user systems do not need intertransaction conflict control, and OCC is not restricted to distributed transactions. Actual conflict frequency matters more than the read-heavy label alone.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries. It works well when conflicts are uncommon, but high contention wastes work on aborts. Multiversion control keeps versions so a reader can use an appropriate snapshot. Snapshot isolation is not automatically serializable: concurrent writes to different rows can violate a shared invariant.ADB16

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — High conflicts cause validation failures and repeated wasted work.

            B · correct — Rare conflicts allow optimistic private work to validate successfully with few retries.

            C · incorrect — A single-user setting lacks the concurrent conflict problem motivating this choice.

            D · incorrect — Optimistic control is not limited to distributed transaction environments.

            Question 202

            Deadlock occurs when:

            • A. One transaction waits for a resource held by no one
            • B. Two or more transactions each wait for resources held by the other in a circular chain
            • C. A transaction commits too slowly
            • D. Multiple transactions read identical data

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 19

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Correct answer: B — A circular resource-wait chain.

            ADB13 requires a waiting cycle: participants hold resources needed by others and cannot make progress without a victim release or another intervention. Waiting for an unheld resource does not state such a cycle. Slow commit and simultaneous reads can occur without deadlock; compatible shared readers in particular need not block one another.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13
            A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.ADB13
            No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.ADB11

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — A resource held by no one does not create the stated circular hold-and-wait dependency.

            B · correct — Each participant waits for another holder in a cycle, preventing independent progress.

            C · incorrect — A slow commit may still progress and need not form a waiting cycle.

            D · incorrect — Compatible shared reads of the same data do not inherently deadlock.

            Question 203

            In the Wait-Die protocol, when a YOUNGER transaction requests a resource held by an OLDER transaction:

            • A. The younger transaction dies (aborts)
            • B. The older transaction dies
            • C. The younger transaction waits
            • D. Both transactions abort

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 20

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Correct answer: A — The younger requester aborts.

            The requester is younger and the holder older. ADB14 makes that requester die in wait–die; only an older requester may wait for a younger holder. On retry the aborted transaction retains its original timestamp. Wounding a holder belongs to a different protocol, and both participants need not be aborted.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.ADB14
            Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive.ADB14
            In wait–die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one; a younger transaction requesting a resource held by an older one aborts.ADB14

            Choice by choice

            A · correct — Wait–die aborts the younger requester when the needed resource is held by an older transaction.

            B · incorrect — The older holder keeps its resource; this protocol does not kill it for a younger requester.

            C · incorrect — Waiting is allowed for an older requester facing a younger holder, not this case.

            D · incorrect — The policy aborts the younger requester, not both participants.

            Question 204

            In the Wound-Wait protocol, when an OLDER transaction requests a resource held by a YOUNGER transaction:

            • A. The older transaction waits
            • B. The younger is wounded (aborted), allowing the older to proceed
            • C. Both transactions are aborted
            • D. A new transaction takes over

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 21

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify requester and holder ages before applying the protocol's action.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Correct answer: B — Abort the younger holder so the older requester can proceed.

            ADB14 says an older requester wounds a younger holder, while a younger requester waits. B is therefore the rule for the given ages. The protocol uses priority to prevent cycles rather than arbitrarily aborting both or handing the work to a new transaction. Any retry should preserve the original timestamp to reduce starvation.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A smaller timestamp means an older transaction. In wait–die, an older requester may wait for a younger holder; a younger requester needing an older holder aborts itself. In wound–wait, an older requester aborts the younger holder; a younger requester waits for the older holder. Always identify requester versus holder before applying the names.ADB14
            Retain the original timestamp when restarting an aborted transaction so it gains relative priority as new transactions arrive.ADB14
            In wait–die, an older transaction may wait for a younger one; a younger transaction requesting a resource held by an older one aborts.ADB14

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — An older requester wounds the younger holder rather than waiting under this policy.

            B · correct — The younger holder is aborted, releasing the resource for the older requester.

            C · incorrect — Aborting both is unnecessary and is not the wound–wait rule.

            D · incorrect — No replacement transaction takes over; the older requester continues after the conflicting holder releases.

            Question 205

            Lock Timeout as a deadlock solution works by:

            • A. Building and analyzing wait-for graphs
            • B. Aborting any transaction that waits longer than a specified time limit
            • C. Locking all items before a transaction starts
            • D. Assigning age-based priorities

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 22

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB14 · Wait–die and wound–wait: compare requester and holder

            Correct answer: B — Abort a transaction whose wait exceeds the configured limit.

            ADB13 defines timeout by excessive wait duration and warns it can mistake slow progress for deadlock. B matches that mechanism. Wait-for graphs detect cycles, conservative locking obtains all locks before execution and age priorities define wait–die/wound–wait decisions. Those are distinct policies rather than implementations of a time limit.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deadlock requires a waiting cycle: T1 holds X and wants Y; T2 holds Y and wants X. In a wait-for graph, an edge Ti→Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. A cycle indicates deadlock under the ordinary lock-wait model. Abort a suitable victim, undo its effects and release its locks; repeat if other cycles remain. Aborting every deadlocked transaction also breaks cycles but wastes more work.ADB13
            A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock.ADB13
            Conservative/static 2PL obtains all needed locks before execution and does not begin while only a subset is available, preventing hold-and-wait deadlock.ADB12

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Graph analysis detects cycles rather than deciding from elapsed lock-wait time.

            B · correct — Timeout aborts a waiting transaction after its configured wait limit is exceeded.

            C · incorrect — Preacquiring all locks is conservative locking rather than timeout handling.

            D · incorrect — Age-based priorities define other prevention policies, not an elapsed-wait threshold.

            Question 206

            A schedule is serializable if:

            • A. All transactions execute one after another with no overlap
            • B. Its concurrent execution produces the same result as some serial execution of those transactions
            • C. All transactions commit at the same time
            • D. No two transactions access the same table

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 23

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Distinguish transaction ordering, conflict conditions and full execution equivalence.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

            Correct answer: B — Equivalent behavior to some serial execution, even if interleaved.

            ADB09 defines a serializable schedule as equivalent to a serial order while permitting interleaving. B matches when same result means the required full transaction equivalence, not an accidental equality of one final value. A describes a serial schedule, which is a special case but not the general definition. Commit simultaneity and disjoint tables are not required.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A serial schedule executes each transaction's operations consecutively. A serializable schedule is equivalent to some serial order; it may interleave transactions. Equality of one final value is insufficient evidence because different executions can accidentally coincide. Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same item and at least one writes. Read/read pairs do not conflict.ADB09

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — This defines serial execution, a stricter special case that omits permitted serializable interleavings.

            B · correct — Serializable behavior is equivalent to some serial ordering; coincidental equality of one value alone is insufficient.

            C · incorrect — Simultaneous commits do not establish the required transaction-execution equivalence.

            D · incorrect — Serializable transactions may access the same tables if their operations are correctly ordered.

            Question 207

            Lock Upgrade refers to:

            • A. Releasing an exclusive lock to a shared lock
            • B. Converting a shared (read) lock to an exclusive (write) lock
            • C. Removing all locks at commit
            • D. Granting a lock to multiple transactions

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 24

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Compare access permissions and same-item compatibility before granting a lock request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Correct answer: B — Convert Shared to Exclusive.

            ADB11 identifies S→X as an upgrade, possible only after incompatible other holders leave. It strengthens an existing read lock to permit writing. X→S is a downgrade, releasing all locks is transaction cleanup and granting compatible readers is shared acquisition. Only B names the requested conversion of a held lock.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A transaction must own the appropriate lock before access and can release only its own locks. S→X is an upgrade, possible only after conflicting other holders leave. X→S is a downgrade. The lock manager decides requests; the lock table stores granted locks and waiting requests. One transaction may request a lock on an already locked item: it is granted if compatible, otherwise waits or aborts under the policy. No double-locking is not a prohibition on shared readers.ADB11

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Exclusive-to-shared is a downgrade rather than an upgrade.

            B · correct — Shared-to-exclusive strengthens the lock to permit writing when compatibility allows.

            C · incorrect — Removing locks is release rather than conversion to a stronger mode.

            D · incorrect — Granting compatible shared readers is not the upgrade of one existing lock.

            Question 208

            Starvation in concurrency control means:

            • A. A transaction holding too many locks
            • B. A transaction is perpetually delayed and never executes due to other transactions always taking priority
            • C. The database runs out of storage space
            • D. A transaction commits before completing all operations

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 25

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Distinguish a waiting cycle, a long wait and indefinite unfair postponement.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB13 · Deadlock detection, prevention and starvation

            Correct answer: B — Indefinite postponement caused by repeated priority to other work.

            ADB13 defines starvation as indefinite postponement while other transactions progress, without requiring a deadlock cycle. B states that repeated bypass precisely. Holding many locks can create contention but does not itself prove starvation. Storage exhaustion and premature commit are different failures, so neither supplies the scheduling-fairness definition.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Fixed resource ordering and conservative 2PL prevent cycles. A no-wait policy aborts immediately on an incompatible lock request and needs no age timestamp. A timeout aborts long waits but may mistake slow progress for deadlock. Starvation is indefinite postponement while other work proceeds, without a required cycle. Fair queues, sensible victim selection and retaining original transaction timestamps on retry reduce starvation; deadlock freedom alone does not prove fairness.ADB13

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Holding many locks describes resource use rather than being perpetually denied execution.

            B · correct — Repeated priority to others can indefinitely postpone the transaction while other work continues.

            C · incorrect — Running out of storage is a capacity failure rather than the defined scheduling starvation.

            D · incorrect — Premature commit concerns transaction correctness rather than indefinite postponement.

            Question 209

            The first step in SQL query processing is:

            • A. Optimization
            • B. Evaluation
            • C. Parsing and Translation
            • D. Result Delivery

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 26

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate query representation, strategy selection and execution.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB17 · Query processing: representation before execution

            Correct answer: C — Parsing and translation.

            ADB17 first checks syntax and semantics and constructs a logical query representation, before optimization and evaluation. C groups those initial activities. Result delivery follows execution, while optimization needs an understood query to compare valid plans. The phase grouping is conventional, but the ordering dependency is explicit in the complete note.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Parsing checks SQL grammar; semantic analysis resolves names, types and access permissions. Translation constructs a logical representation, typically relational algebra or a logical query tree. Optimization chooses equivalent operations, join order and physical access methods. Evaluation executes that plan and returns results. Not every implementation exposes exactly the same phase boundaries.ADB17
            Query processing is the whole activity; selecting a suitable efficient strategy is optimization.ADB17
            DDL is not a mandatory stage before each SELECT, so authentication→DDL→DML permutations do not describe the processing sequence.ADB17

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Optimization follows understanding and representing the query rather than preceding it.

            B · incorrect — Evaluation executes a selected plan and is not the first processing activity.

            C · correct — Parsing/translation establishes query meaning and logical representation before optimization.

            D · incorrect — Results can be delivered only after the required evaluation produces them.
