            Question 211

            What does query optimization aim to minimize?

            • A. The number of tables referenced
            • B. The overall cost (time and resources) of executing the query
            • C. The number of join operations
            • D. The character length of the SQL query

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 28

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Correct answer: B — Overall execution cost under the chosen resource model.

            ADB19 measures candidate plans using I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. The aim is a suitable low-cost equivalent plan, not syntactic brevity or indiscriminate removal of joins and tables. Required tables and semantics must be preserved; even fewer operations do not necessarily imply lower runtime or resource cost.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A cost model estimates resources for a candidate plan: page I/O, CPU, memory, temporary storage and network traffic. Catalog statistics include row/page counts, distinct values and distributions. Selection with fraction s predicts s×N rows. For non-NULL equijoin keys, a common estimate is |R|×|S|/max(V(R,k),V(S,k)), assuming uniform values and containment of the smaller distinct-value domain within the larger. Adjust counts for NULLs; if either non-NULL input is empty, the result is zero. Skew, correlations or incomplete domain overlap can invalidate this estimate; known disjoint domains give zero matches.ADB19
            Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans.ADB19
            For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time.ADB19

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Required tables cannot be discarded merely to reduce the table count.

            B · correct — Optimization compares equivalent plans using estimated time and resource costs.

            C · incorrect — Join count alone ignores access paths, cardinalities and the cost of each join.

            D · incorrect — Short SQL text does not necessarily produce a cheaper execution plan.

            Question 212

            The dominant cost factor in query execution is typically:

            • A. CPU processing time
            • B. Network transmission time
            • C. Disk I/O time (seek + transfer)
            • D. Memory allocation time

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 29

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Correct answer: C — Disk I/O in the conventional local-disk query-cost model.

            ADB19 says disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples, matching the question’s typical teaching model. C includes both seek and transfer work. This is a contextual tendency, not a universal claim: CPU can dominate in-memory work and communication can dominate distributed plans. The answer should retain that local-disk qualification rather than extend it to every system.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.ADB19

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — CPU can dominate in-memory work but is not the typical local-disk-model answer.

            B · incorrect — Network cost can dominate distributed plans rather than the conventional local-disk model.

            C · correct — Seek and transfer I/O often dominate the conventional disk-based cost model.

            D · incorrect — Memory allocation is not the dominant term specified for the textbook local-disk model.

            Question 213

            If a query requires 5 seeks (tS=5ms each) and transfers 10 blocks (tT=1ms each), what is the disk I/O cost?

            • A. 50ms
            • B. 35ms
            • C. 15ms
            • D. 25ms

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 30

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify the resource objective, counts and unit costs before comparing execution strategies.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB19 · Estimate costs, cardinalities and selectivity

            Correct answer: B — 35 ms.

            ADB19 adds seeks times seek duration to blocks times per-block transfer duration. Five seeks cost 5×5=25 ms and ten block transfers cost 10×1=10 ms. Their sum is 35 ms. The terms must be added, not multiplied together or considered separately; this is the supplied simple disk model rather than a measured universal query runtime.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            For a simple rotating-disk model, cost = seeks×seek_time + transferred_blocks×block_transfer_time. Five seeks at 5 ms plus ten blocks at 1 ms cost 35 ms. Disk I/O often dominates textbook local-disk examples; CPU can dominate in-memory work and network can dominate distributed plans. State the assumed cost objective before ranking strategies.ADB19

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Fifty does not equal the sum of 25 ms seeking and 10 ms transfer.

            B · correct — Five times five plus ten times one gives 35 ms.

            C · incorrect — Fifteen omits the correct five-seek multiplication.

            D · incorrect — Twenty-five counts only seek time and omits ten milliseconds of transfer.

            Question 214

            Database recovery restores the database after failure to:

            • A. Its state at database creation
            • B. A consistent and correct state, undoing incomplete transactions and reapplying committed ones
            • C. The state at the last user login
            • D. An empty state for fresh start

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 31

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify what failed, what durable resources survive and which restoration action is required.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Correct answer: B — A valid recovered state preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.

            ADB26 defines restart recovery by preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects after failure. B matches the simple undo/redo teaching model. The detailed work depends on buffer policy and algorithm; not every committed update needs physical redo if already installed. Recovery does not reset the database to creation, last login or an empty replacement state.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Transaction failures include invalid operations, constraint violations and concurrency-control aborts. Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure. A system crash loses volatile memory while disks may survive. Media failure damages persistent storage and normally requires restoring a backup, then replaying available archived logs. Human mistakes may require point-in-time restoration before the bad committed operation.ADB26
            Restart recovery restores a valid database after a crash while preserving durable commits and removing incomplete effects.ADB26
            In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners.ADB27

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Returning to creation would discard legitimate later durable commits.

            B · correct — Recovery preserves committed work and removes incomplete effects to restore valid state.

            C · incorrect — User login time is not the transaction recovery boundary.

            D · incorrect — Emptying the database would destroy committed data rather than recover it.

            Question 215

            Which type of failure occurs when DBMS software bugs cause unexpected behavior?

            • A. Hardware Failure
            • B. Natural Disaster
            • C. Software Error
            • D. Network Failure

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 32

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Classify the stated cause rather than inferring it from the observed symptom.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB-S05 · Classify a failure by its stated cause

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB-S05 · Classify a failure by its stated cause

            ADB26 · Classify failures and choose the starting resource

            Correct answer: C — Software error.

            The stem directly identifies DBMS software bugs as the cause. That is a software error rather than failed hardware, a natural event or broken communication. ADB26 separates transaction/system/media failure concerns so the recovery resource can be chosen appropriately; an observed crash alone would not identify its cause, but this question explicitly supplies it.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A software failure originates in erroneous program behavior, such as a logical programming defect, invalid operation or operating-system fault. A hardware failure originates in malfunctioning physical equipment; loss of disk contents is media failure. An accidental user deletion is human error even if the software executes the requested command correctly. Physical catastrophes such as fire can also cause failure. The observed symptom of a crash does not alone identify which cause occurred.ADB-S05
            Generic recovery-manager terminology should not be mistaken for an exact MySQL component specification.ADB26
            Enforcing concurrency can deliberately abort work; it does not prevent every transaction failure.ADB26

            D · incorrect — No failed network connection is given as the cause of the behavior.

            Question 216

            What does WAL require? In B, 'corresponding data changes' specifically means durable output of the changed data page; volatile buffer changes may occur earlier.

            • A. Data written to disk before the log record
            • B. Log records written to stable storage BEFORE corresponding data changes
            • C. Logs written only after transaction commits
            • D. Checkpoints before every write operation

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 33

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            Correct answer: B — B. Log records written to stable storage BEFORE corresponding data changes

            The update log needed for recovery must be stable before the changed data page becomes persistent. B states that order under the question's explicit durable-write meaning. The buffer can be modified earlier. Data-before-log reverses the rule, waiting until after commit is not the required logging policy and checkpointing before every write is not a WAL requirement.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Write-ahead logging requires the update log needed for recovery to reach stable storage before the corresponding changed data page reaches disk. To acknowledge a durable commit, force the transaction's required log records, including its commit record, to stable storage. A buffer can be changed before that log flush; WAL orders durable writes, not every CPU assignment.ADB27
            Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not.ADB27
            Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward.ADB27

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — The durable log must precede the changed page, not follow it.

            B · correct — With the stated scope, stable logs precede corresponding durable page output.

            C · incorrect — Update logging is not deferred until after commit.

            D · incorrect — WAL does not require a checkpoint for every write.

            Question 217

            The Redo operation during recovery:

            • A. Reverses incomplete transactions
            • B. Re-applies committed transactions whose changes were not yet persisted to disk
            • C. Creates new checkpoints
            • D. Locks data items during the recovery process

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 34

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Correct answer: B — Reapply missing logged committed effects in the simple undo/redo model.

            ADB27 uses redo to install logged after-images when necessary. B describes preserving committed work missing from disk pages in the simple teaching model. It does not mean re-running application side effects or blindly adding an amount twice. ARIES has a broader repeat-history phase before undo, but that does not make reversal, checkpoint creation or lock acquisition the definition of redo.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.ADB27
            In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo.ADB30
            Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.ADB30

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Reversing incomplete changes is undo rather than redo.

            B · correct — Redo installs required logged effects missing from data pages, preserving committed work in the simple model.

            C · incorrect — Checkpoint creation records recovery state rather than reapplying update after-images.

            D · incorrect — Locking may coordinate access but is not the operation of logged redo.

            Question 218

            The Undo operation during recovery:

            • A. Re-applies committed transactions
            • B. Reverses changes of incomplete/aborted transactions using before-images from the log
            • C. Writes the WAL to stable storage
            • D. Creates shadow page copies

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 35

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track durable-write ordering and distinguish reversing incomplete work from installing logged effects.

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB27 · WAL, undo and redo

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            Correct answer: B — Restore before-images of incomplete or aborted work.

            ADB27 restores before-images when undoing incomplete effects, normally following that transaction’s updates backward. B states both the affected work and the supporting log information. Applying committed after-images is redo, forcing logs is a WAL durability action, and copying pages is part of a different update/recovery approach. None is the reversal operation itself.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Undo restores before-images of incomplete effects, usually traversing that transaction's updates backward. Redo installs logged after-images when necessary, usually forward. Setting X to its logged after-value is idempotent; blindly replaying X=X+10 twice is not. In a simple undo/redo teaching model, undo losers and redo winners. ARIES has a different redo phase that repeats history before undoing losers.ADB27
            It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.ADB29
            Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.ADB29

            A · incorrect — Reapplying committed effects is the redo purpose in the simple model.

            B · correct — Undo restores logged old values to remove incomplete or aborted transaction effects.

            C · incorrect — Forcing the log supports durable ordering but does not itself reverse data changes.

            D · incorrect — Shadow-page copies preserve versions instead of defining logged before-image undo.

            Question 219

            Shadow Paging recovery technique works by:

            • A. Using timestamps to sequence recovery
            • B. Writing changes to shadow (copy) pages, keeping originals intact, then swapping on commit
            • C. Using transaction logs for all rollbacks
            • D. Taking checkpoints every transaction

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 36

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB15 · Basic timestamp ordering: execute the tests

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            Correct answer: B — Copy changed pages and atomically install the new durable map on commit.

            ADB29 keeps the committed page map unchanged while modifications use new locations and a modified map. Commit durably installs the new root/map pointer after required pages are durable. B captures that preservation-and-switch mechanism. Timestamp ordering, mandatory per-transaction checkpoints and universal log-based rollback are not the defining shadow-paging steps.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            In-place update overwrites the original location. Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version. Shadow paging keeps an unchanged committed page map and a modified map; commit durably installs a new root/map pointer atomically after required pages are durable. Before commit, a crash uses the old map. It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.ADB29
            Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.ADB30
            A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history.ADB30

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Timestamp ordering controls concurrent operations rather than defining shadow page-map replacement.

            B · correct — Copy-on-write preserves originals and commit safely installs the new page map.

            C · incorrect — Shadow paging is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, not mandatory logged rollback for all changes.

            D · incorrect — A checkpoint every transaction is not the mechanism that preserves the old page map.

            Question 220

            A checkpoint in database recovery helps because:

            • A. It stops all transactions
            • B. Recovery can start from the checkpoint state rather than processing the entire log from the beginning
            • C. It creates a full database backup copy
            • D. It grants exclusive locks to all active transactions

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 37

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            Correct answer: B — A checkpoint supplies recovery state that avoids scanning all historical logs from the beginning.

            ADB30 uses durable checkpoint state to avoid processing all old history. B describes that benefit if start means entering recovery analysis, not assuming every earlier update is irrelevant. Active transactions can span a checkpoint and fuzzy-checkpoint redo may require earlier log positions. A checkpoint is not a full backup, universal stop or lock grant.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.ADB30
            Recovery may start analysis at the checkpoint but redo from an earlier required log position.ADB30
            A checkpoint is neither a full backup nor an automatic commit of active transactions.ADB30

            A · incorrect — Fuzzy checkpoints permit ongoing transactions, so stopping all work is not required.

            B · correct — Recorded recovery state provides a bounded starting point, while earlier necessary undo/redo must still be considered.

            C · incorrect — A checkpoint stores recovery metadata and is not a full separate database backup.

            D · incorrect — Checkpointing does not grant every active transaction exclusive locks.

            Question 221

            Under conventional deferred update with no-force, which recovery classifications describe the policy? Select all that apply. Interpret NO UNDO / REDO as 'no undo, redo required'.

            • A. UNDO/REDO
            • B. UNDO only
            • C. REDO only
            • D. NO UNDO / REDO

            Adapted from

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 38

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB28 · Steal and force determine recovery work

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB28 · Steal and force determine recovery work

            Correct answers (select all): C, D — C. REDO only; D. NO UNDO / REDO

            Because uncommitted changes have not reached the persistent database, crash recovery does not need to undo them there. No-force permits committed changes to remain uninstalled, so redo may be required. REDO only and NO UNDO / REDO express the same classification under the stated notation. Undo-only and undo/redo both assert an undo requirement that this deferred model avoids.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.ADB29
            Force writes a transaction's updated data pages at commit; no-force permits committed dirty pages to remain buffered, hence recovery may need redo.ADB28
            Steal permits a page with uncommitted changes to be written to disk; hence recovery may need undo.ADB28

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Usual deferred update does not require undo of uncommitted persistent database changes.

            B · incorrect — Undo only gives the opposite recovery requirement from the usual deferred no-force model.

            C · correct — REDO only is the usual deferred-update recovery classification.

            D · correct — NO UNDO/REDO is another spelling of the same redo-only requirement.

            Study-guide references

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB-S01 · Query representations and relational operators

            Correct answer: B — UNION.

            Horizontal fragments contain selected subsets of the original relation’s rows. ADB36 reconstructs the relation by their union, assuming completeness and the intended overlap rules. Joining is used to align vertical column pieces by a key; intersection would keep only shared rows and difference would remove rows, so neither reconstructs all horizontal fragments.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
            Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.ADB36
            A relation is represented by a table of tuples.ADB-S01

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Key joins reconstruct matching vertical column pieces, not ordinary horizontal row partitions.

            B · correct — Union collects the rows from every complete horizontal fragment.

            C · incorrect — Intersection keeps only common rows and would discard rows unique to individual fragments.

            D · incorrect — Difference removes rows instead of recombining all fragment members.

            Question 229

            Vertical fragmentation divides a table by:

            • A. Rows
            • B. Columns (attributes), with primary key repeated in each fragment
            • C. Number of concurrent transactions
            • D. Geographic location of data

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 46

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            Correct answer: B — Column subsets with a repeated key or row identifier.

            ADB36 splits a relation by columns and repeats a key or row identifier so the pieces can be joined without spurious matches. B describes that usual primary-key form. Rows are split horizontally; transaction counts and geography concern workload or placement rather than the attribute-level split defining vertical fragmentation. The shared identifier can be an appropriate equivalent key.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
            Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.ADB36
            Reconstruct by reversing the operations: key joins for corresponding vertical pieces and unions for horizontal pieces.ADB36

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Row subsets define horizontal rather than vertical fragmentation.

            B · correct — Vertical fragments contain column subsets plus a repeated identifier for reconstruction.

            C · incorrect — Concurrent transaction count is a workload property rather than the dimension being split.

            D · incorrect — Geographic placement does not define the column projection used for vertical fragments.

            Question 230

            Full replication in distributed databases has which disadvantage?

            • A. Low data availability
            • B. Every update must be applied to all copies, creating high overhead
            • C. Fast read performance
            • D. Simple concurrency control

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 47

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate copy placement, propagation timing and update-maintenance cost.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Correct answer: B — Propagating each update across all copies adds maintenance overhead.

            ADB37 says copies improve locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. B names that maintenance burden for full replication. Propagation timing may be synchronous or asynchronous, so the answer does not imply every copy is updated simultaneously. Fast reads are a possible benefit, and concurrency control becomes more involved rather than inherently simple.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Full replication places the whole database at every relevant site; partial replication copies selected fragments to selected sites; nonredundant allocation stores each fragment once. Copies improve read locality and can improve availability but require storage and update propagation. They can also spread mistakes, so replication does not replace independent backups.ADB37
            Full replication does not inherently mean every copy is updated simultaneously; its synchronization rule must be stated.ADB37
            Lazy/asynchronous replication propagates later and may expose stale reads or need conflict resolution.ADB37

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Usable replicas can improve availability rather than inherently making it low.

            B · correct — All copies must eventually reflect relevant updates, creating propagation and coordination overhead.

            C · incorrect — Fast reads are a potential benefit rather than the listed disadvantage.

            D · incorrect — Maintaining consistent copies does not inherently simplify concurrency control.

            Question 231

            Fragmentation transparency in distributed databases means:

            • A. Users can see all the fragmentation details
            • B. Users interact with the database as a single entity, unaware of fragmentation existence
            • C. Only DBAs know about fragments
            • D. Fragments are listed as separate tables in the schema

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 48

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify exactly which detail is hidden from the user.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

            Correct answer: B — Users query the logical relation without knowing its fragments.

            ADB35 defines fragmentation transparency as hiding the existence and reconstruction of fragments. B states that user-facing abstraction directly. It does not require literally only DBAs to know the implementation; developers and administrators may also need that knowledge. Exposing fragment tables or all fragmentation details to users would make fragmentation visible instead of transparent.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Location transparency hides which site holds a named object. Fragmentation transparency hides the existence and reconstruction of fragments: users query the whole logical relation. Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained. The broad single-logical-database experience may involve all three.ADB35
            If users explicitly name a fragment but need not specify its site, fragmentation is visible while location can remain transparent.ADB35
            Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation.ADB35

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Showing all fragmentation details is the opposite of hiding them from ordinary queries.

            B · correct — Users operate on the whole logical relation without managing its fragment reconstruction.

            C · incorrect — Transparency describes the user abstraction, not exclusive knowledge restricted to DBAs alone.

            D · incorrect — Naming fragments separately exposes fragmentation rather than concealing it from the querying user.

            Question 232

            The Middleware architecture in distributed DBMS uses:

            • A. Direct client-to-server connections
            • B. All servers collaborating on every query
            • C. A dedicated middleware server that mediates between clients and multiple independent database servers
            • D. A single centralized database server

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 49

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify which tier submits, mediates or executes a request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            Correct answer: C — Middleware mediates between clients and independent database servers.

            ADB34 lets middleware translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. C describes that mediating tier. The logical responsibility does not require exactly one physical machine in every implementation. Direct connections omit this mediator, universal server collaboration is a different arrangement, and one centralized server is not the stated distributed middleware design.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules. In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions. Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.ADB34

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Direct client-server links alone omit the middleware mediation that defines the requested architecture.

            B · incorrect — Every server need not participate in every query; relevant sources depend on the request.

            C · correct — A middleware tier mediates client requests across multiple independent database servers.

            D · incorrect — One centralized database server does not describe mediation across independent distributed servers.

            Question 233

            Hybrid fragmentation combines which two techniques?

            • A. Full replication and no replication
            • B. Horizontal fragmentation and vertical fragmentation
            • C. Locking and timestamp-based concurrency control
            • D. Client-server and middleware architectures

            Source

            • Advanced Database Systems review questions · Question 50

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            Correct answer: B — Horizontal and vertical fragmentation.

            ADB36 explicitly defines hybrid fragmentation as combining row and column splits in an appropriate order. B names those two operations. Replication changes copy placement, locking and timestamps control concurrent access, and client-server/middleware describe architecture responsibilities. They can coexist with hybrid fragmentation but are not its two component fragmentation techniques.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
            Hybrid fragmentation combines row and column splits in either suitable order.ADB36
            These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.ADB34

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Full/no replication concerns copies rather than the row and column splits of hybrid fragmentation.

            B · correct — Hybrid fragmentation combines horizontal row subsets with vertical column subsets.

            C · incorrect — Locking and timestamps are concurrency-control mechanisms, not fragmentation types.

            D · incorrect — These are architecture forms rather than the two data-fragmentation operations.

            Question 234

            In client-server database architecture, what is the primary role of the server?

            • A. Provide the GUI for end users
            • B. Initiate all network connections and poll clients for updates
            • C. Store and manage shared data, enforce ACID properties, and process client requests
            • D. Cache all user sessions locally for offline access

            Source

            • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 3

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify which tier submits, mediates or executes a request.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB34 · Architectures and local autonomy

            ADB06 · Transactions, ACID and state transitions

            Correct answer: C — Manage shared data, process requests and enforce supported transaction/integrity guarantees.

            ADB34 assigns clients request submission and servers shared-data management, operation execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement. C matches those responsibilities. User interfaces usually belong to clients, while initiating all connections, polling every client or caching all sessions for offline use are not the server role defined by this architecture. Guarantees still depend on supported mechanisms and correct application use.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            In client/server architecture, clients submit requests while servers manage shared data, execute operations and enforce supported integrity/transaction rules. In collaborating-server designs, servers cooperate on subqueries and transactions. Middleware can translate requests, locate data, coordinate operations and combine results across independent servers. These describe communication responsibilities, not fragmentation types.ADB34
            Calling a system heterogeneous does not require all sites to surrender autonomy or to copy every row everywhere.ADB34
            A tightly integrated distributed system can present one global schema and shared control.ADB34

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — The user-facing GUI is normally a client responsibility rather than the database server's primary role.

            B · incorrect — The server need not initiate every connection or poll clients for every update.

            C · correct — Shared-data management, query execution and supported integrity/transaction enforcement are server duties.

            D · incorrect — Caching every session for offline access is not the defined database-server responsibility.

            Question 235

            In two-phase locking (2PL), during which phase may a transaction acquire locks but not release any?

            • A. Growing phase
            • B. Commit phase
            • C. Validation phase
            • D. Shrinking phase

            Source

            • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 5

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Track the first lock release and the transaction-completion boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB12 · Two-phase locking and its variants

            ADB16 · Optimistic control, versions and lock granularity

            Correct answer: A — Growing phase.

            ADB12 allows acquiring or upgrading locks during growing and releasing or downgrading them during shrinking. Once any lock is released, a transaction may not acquire another. A is therefore the phase described. Commit is a transaction event, validation belongs to optimistic control and shrinking has the opposite lock-release role.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Basic 2PL has a growing phase that acquires/upgrades locks and a shrinking phase that releases/downgrades them. Once any lock is released, no new lock may be acquired. The lock point is the instant the final lock is obtained. 2PL guarantees conflict serializability for well-formed transactions, but can deadlock and basic 2PL alone need not prevent cascading aborts.ADB12
            Two-phase locking orders access to data; two-phase commit coordinates a distributed commit decision.ADB12
            Optimistic/validation control reads and computes privately, validates its read/write sets against overlapping transactions, then publishes if validation succeeds; otherwise it retries.ADB16

            Choice by choice

            A · correct — Growing permits acquisitions and upgrades before any release starts.

            B · incorrect — Commit is not the general 2PL phase for new lock acquisition.

            C · incorrect — Validation is an optimistic-control stage rather than the 2PL growing phase.

            D · incorrect — Shrinking releases or downgrades locks and forbids acquiring new ones.

            Question 236

            Assume that we are able to specify that Mr. Getahun can view the database record, but cannot change the value of the record. Which security management technique was used in this scenario?

            • A. Access Control
            • B. Availability
            • C. Non-repudiation
            • D. Integrity

            Source

            • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 27

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify whether the scenario concerns identity, permission, disclosure or valid values.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            ADB-S03 · Availability and evidence against false denial

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB24 · Security, integrity and inference control

            ADB-S03 · Availability and evidence against false denial

            Correct answer: A — Access control.

            ADB24 explicitly describes a user allowed to view but not change a record as having restricted access privileges. That is authorization/access control. Integrity concerns valid values, availability concerns readiness for use and non-repudiation concerns attributable actions rather than whether a particular read or write is permitted. A matches the actual permission distinction.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Authentication establishes identity; authorization/access control determines permitted actions. Encryption protects stored or transmitted content; integrity constraints restrict valid data; auditing records actions. A user who can view but cannot change a record has restricted access privileges. A view can restrict visible rows/columns, but its privilege and execution rules must support that restriction.ADB24
            Neither property specifies which particular user has permission to change a database row; that is the separate authorization decision.ADB-S03
            Availability concerns keeping services and resources accessible to their authorized users.ADB-S03

            Choice by choice

            A · correct — Access control grants reading while denying modification for the specified user.

            B · incorrect — Availability concerns service readiness rather than the read-versus-write privilege distinction.

            C · incorrect — Non-repudiation does not define whether this user is authorized to modify a record.

            D · incorrect — Integrity restricts valid data states rather than assigning user-specific read/update permissions.

            Question 237

            Suppose, a developer proposes using deferred update with no checkpoints in a high- transaction OLTP system. What is the most serious drawback?

            • A. Log scans become prohibitively expensive after long uptime
            • B. Increased disk I/O due to frequent page copying
            • C. Shared locks cannot be used
            • D. View serializability cannot be ensured

            Source

            • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 28

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify which history a recovery boundary can safely exclude and whether active work spans it.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB30 · Checkpoints and recovery boundaries

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB11 · Locks, compatibility, conversion and managers

            ADB09 · Serial schedules, conflicts and precedence graphs

            Correct answer: A — Long-running log scans can make recovery expensive.

            ADB30 warns that without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, a long-running system may scan expensive amounts of log history. Deferred update removes uncommitted persistent effects but does not remove that search problem. Page copying belongs to shadow approaches, while shared locks and serializability are independent concurrency concerns rather than consequences of omitting checkpoints.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            A checkpoint records enough durable recovery state to avoid scanning all old history. In a simple quiescent/checkpoint exercise, specified flushing may make earlier committed work unnecessary to redo. Active transactions can span the checkpoint, so their relevant earlier updates can still need undo. Do not assume every transaction before a checkpoint needs no processing.ADB30
            Without checkpoints or another valid truncation boundary, long-running systems may need expensive log scans; deferred update does not avoid that problem.ADB30
            Shadow/copy-on-write update writes a new location while preserving the committed version.ADB29

            Choice by choice

            A · correct — High transaction volume and long uptime can produce costly recovery log scans without a valid boundary.

            B · incorrect — Frequent copy-on-write pages characterize shadow updating rather than the absence of checkpoints in deferred update.

            C · incorrect — Omitting checkpoints does not inherently prohibit shared locks.

            D · incorrect — View serializability is a concurrency-order property, not inherently lost by this checkpoint omission.

            Question 238

            Which listed techniques use transaction logs for recovery under the course model? Interpret Deferred Database Modification as conventional logged deferred update with no-force. Select all that apply.

            • A. Recovery in Multi-database Systems
            • B. ARIES Recovery Algorithm
            • C. Shadow Paging Technique
            • D. Deferred Database Modification

            Adapted from

            • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 46

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Separate update timing from update location and follow the commit boundary.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB31 · ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB29 · Deferred, immediate, in-place and shadow updates

            ADB31 · ARIES and repeated crashes during recovery

            Correct answers (select all): B, D — B. ARIES Recovery Algorithm; D. Deferred Database Modification

            ARIES relies on WAL and log-driven analysis, redo and undo. Conventional logged deferred update also uses recorded updates for redo of committed work, with no undo of uncommitted persistent changes. Both therefore belong to the requested category. Shadow paging preserves old page mappings instead, while recovery in multidatabase systems names an environment rather than a particular log-based technique.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Deferred update keeps uncommitted changes outside the persistent database; in the usual no-force setting it is NO-UNDO/REDO. Redo-only and NO-UNDO/REDO mean the same thing, so those cannot be separate unique answers. Immediate update allows persistent changes before commit and therefore may require undo; it need not flush every write_item immediately.ADB29
            ARIES uses WAL, page log sequence numbers (pageLSN), a transaction table and a dirty-page table.ADB31
            It is an alternative to conventional log-based recovery, with allocation, fragmentation and concurrency costs; it is not primarily a special action done only during recovery.ADB29

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Multidatabase recovery describes an environment rather than one specific recovery technique.

            B · correct — ARIES explicitly uses WAL and log-driven analysis, redo and undo.

            C · incorrect — Shadow paging preserves committed page maps rather than being the conventional log-based technique.

            D · correct — Deferred modification can use logged changes for redo after commitment.

            Question 239

            Which type of fragmentation divides a relation into subrelations containing subsets of its columns, repeating a key or row identifier so the original rows can be reconstructed?

            • A. Replication
            • B. Location
            • C. Horizontal
            • D. Vertical

            Adapted from

            • Computer Science Exit Exam · 2018 · Question 82

            Hint / Module Reference (Where to Read)

            Identify whether rows or columns are split and reverse the split to reconstruct the original relation.

            Study-guide sections

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Answer & Detailed Explanation

            Study-guide references

            ADB36 · Fragmentation: correctness and reconstruction

            ADB35 · Transparency: what exactly is hidden?

            ADB37 · Replication policies and their costs

            Correct answer: D — D. Vertical

            Vertical fragmentation divides a relation by columns. Repeating a key or row identifier allows corresponding pieces to be joined back into the original rows without spurious matches. Horizontal fragmentation divides rows instead. Replication creates copies, while location transparency hides where data resides. Hiding a column split would be fragmentation transparency, but the question asks for the split operation itself.

            Evidence in the complete study note

            Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets by predicates; their union reconstructs the relation. Check completeness so every original row is represented and disjointness if no overlap is intended. Define an explicit fragment for NULL/other values when needed. Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets and repeats a key or row identifier so joining on it reconstructs the original rows without spurious matches.ADB36
            Hiding this column split from queries is fragmentation transparency; the split itself is a data-design operation.ADB35
            Replication transparency hides which copy is used and how copies are maintained.ADB35

            Choice by choice

            A · incorrect — Replication copies data rather than dividing its columns.

            B · incorrect — Location transparency hides sites rather than splitting a relation.

            C · incorrect — Horizontal fragmentation selects row subsets.

            D · correct — Vertical fragmentation projects column subsets with a reconstruction identifier.
